front.title: Regulatory Spectrum Discrete Global Grid System (RSDGGS)

abstract.t: This document defines the Regulatory Spectrum Discrete Global Grid System (RSDGGS), a hierarchical geographic indexing scheme designed to encode the regulatory jurisdiction applicable to Industrial, Scientific, and Medical (ISM) radio band usage at any location on Earth.

RSDGGS represents geographic location as a variable-length byte array of 1 to 8 octets. The length of the array implicitly encodes the spatial resolution of the index, eliminating the need for an explicit resolution field. Truncation of the array yields a coarser representation, enabling privacy-preserving location compaction without loss of structural integrity.

The grid is rooted in a spherical dodecahedron whose twelve pentagonal faces are aligned to approximate the three ITU Radio Regions, with face indices 1, 2, and 3 corresponding directly to ITU Regions 1, 2, and 3 respectively. Each face is recursively subdivided using a hierarchy of isosceles golden gnomon triangles, with 2-bit child indices packed into successive octets.

The system supports both fixed IoT deployments for automated regulatory provisioning during manufacturing and mobile IoT devices that acquire regulatory context through GPS, tethered devices, or peer-assisted discovery. A beacon mechanism is defined whereby location-aware devices broadcast their RSDGGS index within ISM band transmissions, enabling location-unaware peers to derive applicable regulatory parameters including frequency allocation, power limits, duty cycle, dwell interval, channelization, and permitted modulation.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Radio devices operating in ISM bands must comply with regulatory requirements specific to their geographic location. These requirements vary significantly across jurisdictions and include constraints on frequency allocation, radiated power, duty cycle, dwell interval, channelization, and permitted modulation schemes. A device deployed globally may encounter any of dozens of distinct regulatory frameworks depending on where it operates.

Existing geographic indexing systems such as Uber H3 , Google S2 , and OpenLocationCode are designed for general-purpose spatial indexing and do not provide a hierarchical structure aligned to regulatory boundaries. They also lack a mechanism for embedding regulatory context within the index itself.

RSDGGS addresses this gap by defining a hierarchical grid whose coarsest level directly encodes ITU Radio Region membership, and whose progressive refinement resolves national and sub-national regulatory jurisdictions at resolutions appropriate to the regulatory complexity of each geographic area.

The variable-length encoding allows a single-octet index to carry sufficient information to determine ISM band availability for the majority of the world's surface area, while the full eight-octet form provides sub-decimeter resolution adequate for the most complex geopolitical edge cases.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals.
RSDGGS: Regulatory Spectrum Discrete Global Grid System. The indexing scheme defined by this document.
Cell: A geographic region represented by an RSDGGS index. The spatial extent of a cell is determined by the length of its index.
Face: One of the twelve pentagonal faces of the spherical dodecahedron forming the coarsest level of the grid hierarchy.
RSL (Resolution Sufficiency Level): The minimum index length, in octets, required to unambiguously identify the regulatory rule set applicable at a given location for a given ISM band.

Rule Set: The complete collection of regulatory parameters applicable to a specific ISM band at a specific location, including frequency bounds, power limits, duty cycle, dwell interval, channelization, and modulation constraints.

Golden Gnomon Triangle: An isosceles triangle with apex angle 36 degrees and base angles 72 degrees each, in which the ratio of leg length to base length equals the golden ratio phi (~1.618). These triangles tile the pentagonal faces of the dodecahedron.

Beacon Device: An IoT device that has determined its regulatory context, either through GPS, tethered smartphone, or prior bootstrap, and broadcasts its RSDGGS index within ISM band transmissions to assist peers.
Naive Device: An IoT device that has not yet determined its regulatory context and performs channel scanning to discover a Beacon Device.

section.name: Motivation and Design Goals
section.t: The design of RSDGGS is driven by the following goals:

G1 — Regulatory Alignment: The coarsest index level MUST correspond to ITU Radio Region boundaries. Face indices 1, 2, and 3 SHALL correspond to ITU Regions 1, 2, and 3 respectively, enabling a single-octet lookup to determine gross band availability for most ISM bands.

G2 — Self-Describing Resolution: The length of the index in octets SHALL implicitly encode its resolution. No explicit resolution field is required. This enables resolution to be communicated through the CBOR byte string length header at zero additional cost.

G3 — Privacy Truncation: Truncating the index from the right SHALL yield a valid, coarser-resolution index. Devices MAY share a truncated index to disclose only the precision required for the intended purpose, protecting precise location from unnecessary disclosure.

G4 — Embedded Deployment: The encoding and decoding algorithms SHALL be implementable in constrained environments with no heap allocation (no_std, no_alloc in Rust; fixed stack in C). The index fits within a uint64_t.

G5 — CBOR Integration: The index SHALL serialize naturally as a CBOR byte string (major type 2), with the CBOR length header providing resolution information to the receiver at no additional encoding cost.

G6 — Peer-Assisted Discovery: Location-unaware devices SHALL be able to derive their applicable regulatory parameters by receiving a beacon from a location-aware peer, using only the ISM channels permitted at the beacon device's location.

G7 — Manufacturing Provisionability: Fixed-deployment IoT devices SHALL be provisionable with their RSDGGS index at manufacturing time, enabling a single hardware SKU to configure itself correctly based on deployment location without firmware variants.

G8 — Decentralized, Infrastructure-Independent Operation: RSDGGS regulatory context discovery MUST NOT require any centralized server, directory, or management system. All mechanisms for a device to acquire its RSDGGS cell index and associated regulatory rule set SHALL be fully operational in the absence of any network infrastructure beyond the device and its immediate radio neighbors. This precludes DHCP, DNS, and any client-server configuration protocol as a required element of the regulatory bootstrap path. In particular, DHCPv6 introduces a single point of failure: if the DHCP server is unavailable, onboarding nodes cannot be configured. RSDGGS instead follows the model of IPv6 SLAAC (Stateless Address Autoconfiguration) and Neighbor Discovery: a device SHALL be able to determine its own regulatory context from the devices around it, with no dependence on reachability to any server. Tethered devices such as smartphones used for provisioning, and infrastructure systems such as manufacturing databases or cloud enrollment services, are permitted as optional accelerators of the bootstrap process but MUST NOT be required for correct operation. A Naive Device with no tethering, no GPS, no DHCP, and no pre-provisioned cell index SHALL converge on a valid regulatory context solely through the peer-assisted mechanism defined in Section 11.

G9 — Extraterrestrial Extensibility: The RSDGGS index format SHALL be extensible to celestial bodies beyond Earth without changing the wire format, adding version bits, or breaking backward compatibility with existing Earth indices. The four most-significant bits of Octet 0 are designated as the celestial body selector, allowing up to 16 independent dodecahedral grids (one per body) to coexist within a single 8-octet index space. A body selector value of 0x0 (Earth) is the default and preserves full backward compatibility: all RSDGGS indices generated before the body selector field was defined decode identically as Earth face indices. This design goal is motivated by the increasing operational relevance of wireless communications on the Moon (Artemis Program), Mars (long-duration missions), and other bodies where radio frequency coordination under the Outer Space Treaty (1967) will require a compact, self-describing location encoding.

section.name: Rationale for the Dodecahedron
section.t: The choice of a regular dodecahedron as the root polyhedron for RSDGGS is determined by two coupled geometric requirements: the need to contain ITU Radio Regions as coherent single-face units at the coarsest resolution level, and the minimization of map projection distortion variance across cell boundaries relative to the triangular-face alternative.

section.name: Face Count and ITU Region Containment
section.t: Two Platonic solids with spherically projected faces are viable candidates for a global regulatory grid: the regular icosahedron (20 equilateral triangular faces) and the regular dodecahedron (12 regular pentagonal faces). The pair are duals of each other on the unit sphere.

The International Telecommunication Union defines three primary Radio Regions. A grid whose coarsest level directly encodes ITU Region membership requires that each Region be representable as a single face, with face indices numerically matching Region numbers. This constraint drives the face count requirement:

figure.artwork:
Icosahedron — 20 triangular faces: Face area ≈ 1/20 of sphere ≈ 25,500,000 km² ITU Region 2 (Americas) area ≈ 24,700,000 km² → Region 2 barely fits in one triangular face → Remaining 17 faces: over-partitions ITU regions at level 0 → 3 faces assigned to ITU Regions; 17 faces available for sub-regions — excessive granularity at coarsest level → Triangle shape forces boundary cuts through regulatory zones at 60-degree corner angles
Dodecahedron — 12 pentagonal faces: Face area ≈ 1/12 of sphere ≈ 42,000,000 km² ITU Region 2 (Americas) area ≈ 24,700,000 km² → Region 2 fits within one pentagonal face with ~17,300,000 km² margin — accommodates coastal and island territories without boundary cuts → 3 faces assigned to ITU Regions (face indices 1, 2, 3) → 9 faces available for sub-region differentiation at level 0: correct cardinality for the 10 major regulatory blocs defined in Section 4.2

section.t: The icosahedron's 20 faces would require fragmenting each ITU Region across multiple faces at the coarsest level, destroying the direct face-to-region correspondence that is a primary design goal (G1) of RSDGGS. The dodecahedron's 12 faces provide the minimum face count that satisfies the ITU Region alignment constraint while leaving sufficient faces for sub-region differentiation.

The 9 extension faces (4 through 11) of the dodecahedron correspond directly to the major regulatory sub-blocs within the three ITU Regions: four for Region 1 (Europe core, Africa West, Africa East, Russia/Central Asia, Middle East), two for Region 2 (South America, Caribbean), and two for Region 3 (South/Southeast Asia, Oceania). This correspondence is exact and natural for the dodecahedron face count; it would be over-specified with 17 icosahedron extension faces.

section.name: Map Projection Distortion at Face Boundaries
section.t: All polyhedral global grids introduce map projection distortion when spherical regions are represented by planar polygons. The distortion is zero at the face center and increases toward the face boundary. For geographic grid systems used in regulatory compliance, the relevant quantity is the distortion variance across the face: specifically, the ratio of maximum distortion (at face corners) to minimum distortion (at edge midpoints). A lower ratio means cells near boundaries experience more uniform distortion, reducing the magnitude of cell shape irregularity in geographic space.

For gnomonic projection (great circles map to straight lines, the natural projection for spherical polygons), the scale factor at angular distance theta from the face center is 1/cos^2(theta). The distortion ratio between the farthest and nearest boundary points of each face type is computed from the angular radii to the vertex and edge midpoint respectively.

figure.artwork:
Icosahedron triangular face: Angular radius, face center to edge midpoint: ~20.9 deg Angular radius, face center to vertex: ~41.8 deg Gnomonic scale at edge midpoint: 1/cos²(20.9°) ≈ 1.15 Gnomonic scale at vertex: 1/cos²(41.8°) ≈ 1.80 Vertex-to-midpoint distance ratio: 2.00 Distortion ratio (vertex/midpoint scale): 1.57
Dodecahedron pentagonal face: Angular radius, face center to edge midpoint: ~31.7 deg Angular radius, face center to vertex: ~41.8 deg Gnomonic scale at edge midpoint: 1/cos²(31.7°) ≈ 1.38 Gnomonic scale at vertex: 1/cos²(41.8°) ≈ 1.80 Vertex-to-midpoint distance ratio: 1.24 Distortion ratio (vertex/midpoint scale): 1.30

section.t: Both polyhedra produce identical maximum distortion at their vertices (~1.80x gnomonic scale factor at ~41.8 degrees angular radius), because the vertices of the dodecahedron and the vertices of its dual icosahedron lie at the same angular distance from their respective face centers on the unit sphere. The critical difference is the vertex-to-edge-midpoint distance ratio: 2.00 for the equilateral triangle versus 1.24 for the regular pentagon.

The consequence for grid cells near the face boundary is that triangular faces concentrate high distortion at sharp 60-degree corners, with a steep distortion gradient between corner-adjacent cells and edge-midpoint-adjacent cells. The 1.57x distortion ratio means cells within one subdivision level of a triangle corner have substantially different shape distortion from cells of the same level near an edge midpoint. This heterogeneity propagates into the subdivision hierarchy: any subdivision level that places a cell boundary near a triangle corner inherits the distortion spike.

Pentagonal faces distribute boundary distortion more uniformly. The 108-degree interior angle of the regular pentagon produces a shallower boundary curvature, and the 1.30x distortion ratio means corner-adjacent cells and edge-midpoint-adjacent cells experience only 30 percent more scale variation. The progressive 4-fold triangular subdivision of each pentagonal sector (Section 4.5) places triangle apices at the face center — a fixed interior point — rather than at face corners, further reducing the population of high-distortion boundary cells in the subdivision hierarchy.

For regulatory compliance applications, distortion at cell boundaries is specifically relevant at the Resolution Sufficiency Level (RSL, Section 8.2): a cell straddling a regulatory border must resolve the boundary accurately. The more uniform distortion of pentagonal faces means RSL cells near national borders embedded in face boundaries have more predictable shape, reducing the error in determining which side of a border a device is on.

section.name: Summary of Design Decision
section.t: The dodecahedron satisfies both requirements that the icosahedron fails: it provides the correct face count for direct ITU Region alignment, and it produces lower distortion variance at face boundaries due to its obtuse pentagonal corner angles and smaller vertex-to-edge-midpoint distance ratio. These properties are intrinsic to the dodecahedral geometry and are not achievable by orientation adjustment of the icosahedron.

section.name: Face Topology and ITU Region Alignment
section.t: The RSDGGS grid is rooted in a regular dodecahedron projected onto the surface of a unit sphere. A regular dodecahedron has twelve pentagonal faces. RSDGGS assigns these faces as follows:

Face indices 1, 2, and 3 carry the ITU Region number directly, establishing a direct correspondence between a single-octet RSDGGS index and ITU Region membership. Extension faces 4 through 11 subdivide the large ITU regions into coherent regulatory blocs whose parent region is encoded in the regulatory database rather than the index itself.
Face 0 is reserved for polar and Antarctic zones, which are subject to ITU Article 48 special coordination procedures rather than national regulatory frameworks.

section.name: Face Center Orientation
section.t: The dodecahedron is constructed as the dual of the unit icosahedron. The twelve face centers of the dodecahedron correspond to the twelve vertices of the icosahedron after normalization to the unit sphere. The icosahedron is defined by the golden ratio phi = (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2, with twelve vertices at the normalized forms of (0, +-1, +-phi), (+-1, +-phi, 0), and (+-phi, 0, +-1).

A three-step rotation is applied to the entire icosahedron to orient the dodecahedron for ITU regulatory alignment. The rotation places icosahedron vertex 8 -- the normalized form of [phi, 0, 1] -- at geographic coordinates (39 degrees North, 98 degrees West), the approximate centroid of the contiguous United States. As a consequence, RSDGGS Face 2, whose center is the centroid of the five icosahedron triangles surrounding vertex 8, lands at approximately (31.43 degrees North, 102.48 degrees West). This orientation minimizes dodecahedron edge intersections across the harmonized FCC / ISED / IFT regulatory zone of North America, satisfying design goal G2.

In the default (unrotated) icosahedron, vertex 8 at [phi, 0, 1] normalizes to latitude arctan(1/phi) = 31.7175 degrees North, longitude 0 degrees (on the prime meridian). The orientation rotation proceeds in three steps applied to every icosahedron vertex:

figure.artwork:
Step 1: rot_z(0) Vertex 8 is already at lon = 0; no-op. Step 2: rot_x(+7.2825 deg) Raise vertex 8 from 31.7175N to 39.0N. Angle = 39.0 - arctan(1/phi) = 7.2825 deg. Step 3: rot_z(-98.0 deg) Place vertex 8 at 98.0W longitude.
rot_x(a): [x, y*cos(a) - z*sin(a), y*sin(a) + z*cos(a)] rot_z(a): [x*cos(a) - y*sin(a), x*sin(a) + y*cos(a), z]
Result after rotation: Vertex 8 (anchor): 39.0000N, 98.0000W Face 2 center: 31.4323N, 102.4796W

section.t: This rotation procedure is normative for the purpose of independently verifying or regenerating the FACE_CENTERS compile-time constants defined in Section 18.2, and for deriving face center coordinates for non-Earth celestial bodies using a different regulatory anchor (Section 5.5). Implementations MUST use the precomputed FACE_CENTERS constants in Section 18.2 for all runtime face assignment. The rotation itself is never performed at runtime.

The in-plane orientation of Face 2's pentagon -- that is, the compass bearings at which its five vertices point when viewed from the face center -- is not a separate parameter and is not independently configurable. It is a direct geometric consequence of the icosahedron's structure once the anchor vertex position is fixed. Icosahedron vertex 8, which dual-maps to Face 2, has five neighbouring triangular faces arranged at azimuths determined by the icosahedron's fixed symmetry. After the three-step rotation places vertex 8 at 39N, 98W, those five neighbouring centroids land at the following fixed geographic positions, forming the pentagon boundary:

figure.artwork:
V0: 67.92N, 116.36W (bearing 351.5 NNW -- interior BC / Alaska border) V1: 40.23N, 57.13W (bearing 63.5 ENE -- mid-North Atlantic) V2: 29.97N, 146.21W (bearing 279.5 WNW -- North Pacific) V3: 2.59S, 118.75W (bearing 207.5 SSW -- Central Pacific) V4: 2.59N, 77.25W (bearing 135.5 SE -- Colombia coast)
Pentagon tilt: ~63.5 deg clockwise from point-up (no vertex due north). Pentagon circumradius: 37.38 degrees of arc from face center.

section.t: This orientation places the entire conterminous United States, all of Canada south of approximately 62 degrees North, Mexico, Cuba, the Bahamas, and most of the Greater Antilles within Face 2, coinciding with the FCC, ISED, and IFT regulatory jurisdictions. Unavoidable boundary crossings include Alaska (crosses into Face 6), Hawaii (Face 9), and Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands (Face 4). These are the minimum achievable boundary exceptions for any dodecahedral face covering the North American regulatory zone. The FACE_PENTAGON_VERTS compile-time constants in Section 18.2 encode these five boundary vertex positions explicitly and are used at runtime during triangle-sector assignment (Section 6.2). No runtime computation of the icosahedron rotation is ever required.

section.name: Pentagonal Face Subdivision
section.t: Each pentagonal face of the dodecahedron is divided into five congruent isosceles triangles by connecting the face center to each of the five pentagon vertices. Each triangle has its apex at the face center and its base along one edge of the pentagon.

This subdivision produces five triangular sectors per face, indexed 0 through 4. The five sectors are identified within the RSDGGS index by a 3-bit field in Octet 1 of the index, with values 5 through 7 reserved.

section.name: Isosceles Triangle Hierarchy
section.t: The isosceles triangles produced by pentagonal subdivision are golden gnomon triangles: the ratio of their leg length to base length equals the golden ratio phi. These triangles admit a natural 4-fold recursive subdivision by connecting the midpoints of all three sides, producing four congruent child triangles.

figure.artwork: apex /\ / \ / 0 \ Child 0: apex sub-triangle /------\ Child 1: left base sub-triangle /\ mid /\ Child 2: right base sub-triangle / \ / \ Child 3: central inverted triangle / 1 \ / 2 \ / \/ \ /--------3--------\

section.t: Child 3, the central inverted triangle, has inverted orientation relative to its parent. This inversion is intrinsic to 4-fold triangle subdivision and must be tracked for correct neighbor computation. Each child triangle is geometrically similar to the parent, scaled by one-half in linear dimension and one-quarter in area.
The 2-bit child index values are defined as follows: 00 denotes the apex child, 01 denotes the left base child, 10 denotes the right base child, and 11 denotes the central inverted child.

section.name: RSDGGS Dodecahedron Net — ISM Band Regulatory Coverage Map
section.t: Figure 1 illustrates the RSDGGS dodecahedron as a cut-and-fold net. The net shows all twelve faces in their correct topological adjacency, with shared fold edges indicated by dashed lines and free cut edges indicated by solid lines with grey glue tabs. Each pentagonal face is rendered using a gnomonic projection centered on that face's sphere center, ensuring that geographic features are continuous across every fold edge: a coastline, national border, or regulatory boundary that crosses from one face to an adjacent face appears as an unbroken line on both faces. Geographic continuity across all eleven fold edges was verified to within 0.006° of arc (numerical precision only).

The world map on each face is colored according to ISM band regulatory allowance. Countries are colored by the sub-GHz ISM band or bands permitted under their national regulatory framework. Where only the 2.4 GHz band is universally allocated (most of Asia/Pacific), a lighter blue-grey fill indicates the absence of sub-GHz ISM allocation. Countries where multiple sub-GHz bands are simultaneously permitted display the primary band as the fill color with diagonal hatching in the secondary band color.

section.name: Net Topology and Construction
section.t: The net uses a topologically valid unfolding of the dodecahedron. All twelve faces remain connected through their shared fold edges; no face requires cutting and reattaching. The net topology was verified against the true 3D dodecahedron face adjacency graph: each pair of faces in the net that shares a fold edge is confirmed to share a geometric edge in the 3D dodecahedron. Construction proceeds by: (1) printing on A3 or US Tabloid stock at 100% scale (do not fit to page); (2) cutting along all solid outer edges; (3) scoring all dashed fold lines firmly with a stylus; (4) folding each face upward along the scored lines; (5) applying adhesive to each grey GLUE tab; and (6) pressing each tab against the inner surface of the mating face. The last fold closes the final seam.

The gnomonic projection used for each face maps great-circle arcs to straight line segments. Since the shared edge between any two adjacent dodecahedron faces lies on a great circle of the sphere, that edge projects as a straight line in both adjacent face projections. After alignment of the shared-edge endpoints, geographic features cross the fold edge continuously without discontinuity, distortion artifact, or gap.

section.name: Octet Array Format
section.t: An RSDGGS index is a byte array of 1 to 8 octets. The interpretation of each octet is as follows:

figure.artwork:
Octet 0: Bits 7-4: Celestial body selector, values 0-15. 0x0 = Earth (default; backward compatible). 0x1 = Moon. 0x2 = Mars. 0x3-0xE = Reserved. 0xF = Reserved. Bits 3-0: Face index [0..11] on the selected body. Values 12-15 are reserved.
Octet 1: Bits 7-5: Triangle index within face, values 0-4. Values 5-7 are reserved. Bits 4-3: Subdivision level 1 (2-bit child index). Bits 2-1: Subdivision level 2 (2-bit child index). Bit 0: Subdivision level 3, most significant bit. (Level 3 LSB is Octet 2 bit 7.)
Octets 2-7: Packed subdivision levels, 2 bits per level, MSB-first. Each octet carries 4 complete levels EXCEPT where a level straddles an octet boundary (levels 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, and 23 each have one bit in the preceding octet and one bit in this octet). See Section 5.3 for the complete bit-field layout.

section.t: When stored as a uint64_t for in-memory computation, Octet 0 occupies the most significant byte (big-endian octet order). Unused bits in the final octet of a given resolution MUST be set to zero.

The four-bit celestial body selector in bits 7-4 of Octet 0 partitions the RSDGGS index space into sixteen independent dodecahedral grids, one per celestial body. Body 0x0 (Earth) is the default and backward-compatible value: all existing RSDGGS indices have Octet 0 in the range 0x00-0x0B, which corresponds to body=0, face=0-11. Implementations that predate this field definition will continue to decode these indices correctly as Earth face indices.

The body selector enables RSDGGS to serve as a unified location encoding for operations on the Moon, Mars, and future celestial bodies where wireless regulatory coordination may be required under the Outer Space Treaty (1967) and subsequent ITU coordination frameworks. The dodecahedral grid geometry is body-agnostic: the same 12-face topology and subdivision hierarchy applies to any approximately spherical body, with face assignments and regulatory databases defined independently per body. New body selector values are assigned by IANA under the "RSDGGS Celestial Body Selector" sub-registry defined in Section 20.

section.name: Privacy Truncation
section.t: An RSDGGS index MAY be truncated to any shorter length to reduce precision. The resulting truncated index is a valid RSDGGS index at the coarser resolution corresponding to its new length. No metadata is lost by truncation, as the resolution is fully recoverable from the length of the remaining bytes.

Implementations sharing location information with peers SHOULD use the minimum resolution necessary for the intended regulatory purpose. For ISM band availability determination, 1 octet is sufficient for most locations. For country-level rule set selection, 3 octets are RECOMMENDED. For border zone and enclave disambiguation, 4 to 6 octets MAY be required.

Implementations MUST NOT infer more precise location information from a truncated index than its resolution supports. The geographic region corresponding to a truncated index is the entire cell at that resolution, not the point within it from which the index was derived.

section.name: Face Assignment
section.t: Given a geographic coordinate (latitude, longitude) in decimal degrees, the face index is determined by finding the dodecahedron face whose center has the maximum dot product with the unit vector corresponding to the coordinate. This is equivalent to finding the nearest face center on the unit sphere.

figure.artwork:
1. Convert (lat, lon) to unit Cartesian vector: x = cos(lat) * cos(lon) y = cos(lat) * sin(lon) z = sin(lat)
2. For each face i in [0..11]: d_i = dot(point, face_center[i])
3. face = argmax(d_i)

section.t: Face centers are precomputed from the rotated icosahedron vertex positions as described in Section 4.3. Implementations SHOULD store all twelve face center vectors as compile-time constants to avoid runtime trigonometric computation on constrained devices.

section.name: Triangle Assignment Within Face
section.t: After determining the face, the coordinate is assigned to one of the five triangular sectors within the face. Each sector is bounded by the face center and two adjacent pentagon vertices. Assignment is performed using spherical excess tests on the unit sphere.

For each of the five triangles T_k (k = 0..4), defined by vertices (face_center, pentagon_vertex_k, pentagon_vertex_{k+1 mod 5}), the point is contained in T_k if and only if it lies on the correct side of all three great-circle arcs bounding the triangle. The side test for an arc defined by two unit vectors A and B is given by the sign of the triple scalar product dot(cross(A, B), P), where P is the point under test.
The pentagon vertex positions for each face are derived from the dodecahedron geometry and MUST be stored as precomputed constants.

section.name: Recursive Subdivision
section.t: Given the face and triangle sector, the coordinate is recursively assigned to child triangles to the depth required by the desired index length. At each level, the three edge midpoints of the current triangle are computed by normalizing the mean of the two endpoint vectors:

figure.artwork:
mid(A, B) = normalize(A + B)
Children of triangle (apex, left, right): Child 0: (apex, mid(apex,left), mid(apex,right)) Child 1: (mid(apex,left), left, mid(left,right)) Child 2: (mid(apex,right), mid(left,right), right ) Child 3: (mid(left,right), mid(apex,right), mid(apex,left)) [inverted orientation]

section.t: The child containing the point is determined by the same spherical excess containment test used in Section 6.2. The 2-bit child index is appended to the index bit stream. This process repeats until the required number of subdivision levels have been encoded.

Implementations targeting constrained environments SHOULD use integer approximations of the normalized midpoint computation, such as fixed-point arithmetic with sufficient precision for the target resolution depth. For resolutions of 4 octets or fewer, 32-bit fixed-point arithmetic is sufficient. For resolutions of 6 octets or greater, 64-bit arithmetic is RECOMMENDED.

section.name: Compact Form
section.t: An RSDGGS index is encoded as a CBOR byte string (major type 2) . The byte string length provides the resolution information at no additional cost, satisfying design goal G5. The compact form is suitable for resource-constrained IoT messages where protocol overhead must be minimized.

figure.artwork: 0x41 0x02 -- 1-byte index, face 2 (ITU Region 2 / N. America) 0x43 0x02 0xA4 0x30 -- 3-byte index, country-level precision 0x48 ... -- 8-byte index, maximum resolution

section.name: Tagged Form
section.t: Implementations requiring explicit type identification SHOULD use a CBOR tag to mark the byte string as an RSDGGS index. A private-use tag in the range 65536-15309735 SHOULD be used pending IANA assignment. The recommended placeholder tag value is 0xC24D52 (pending registration).

section.name: Band Entry Schema
section.t: The regulatory database maps RSDGGS cells to rule sets. Each rule set entry contains the complete regulatory parameters for one ISM band in one jurisdiction. Regulatory databases are body-specific: an Earth database contains only Earth cell indices (Octet 0 body selector = 0x0), and a future Lunar database would contain only Lunar cell indices (body selector = 0x1). Implementations MUST NOT apply an Earth regulatory database to a non-Earth RSDGGS index. The body selector in Octet 0 MUST be checked before any database lookup, and an unknown body selector MUST result in an error response rather than a default or fallback regulatory rule set. section.name: Resolution Sufficiency Levels
section.t: The Resolution Sufficiency Level (RSL) for a given face and band specifies the minimum index length at which the regulatory rule set is unambiguous. Devices MUST acquire an index of at least RSL octets before performing a regulatory lookup for that band.

For faces where a band is universally illegal, RSL 1 is sufficient: the face byte alone enables immediate determination that the band is unavailable, and no further index bytes are required for regulatory validation purposes.

section.name: Exception Overlay Table
section.t: Certain jurisdictions cannot be fully resolved by the regular grid at any practical resolution due to their small geographic extent, enclave status, or face-level regulatory misassignment. These locations are addressed by an exception overlay table consulted after the primary database lookup when the band-entry exception flag is set.

section.name: Regulatory Database Validity Limitations
section.t: The regulatory database embedded in an RSDGGS implementation is a point-in-time snapshot of applicable regulations at the time of compilation or last update. Implementers and operators MUST be aware of the following limitations inherent to any static regulatory database.

Regulatory change: National spectrum regulations, ITU Radio Regulation allocations, and bilateral coordination agreements change over time through legislative action, treaty revision, ITU World Radiocommunication Conference (WRC) decisions, and emergency administrative orders. A database that was accurate at device manufacture may no longer correctly represent the regulatory environment at the time of deployment. RSDGGS provides no mechanism to detect or signal database staleness; this is an architectural limitation of the static-database approach required by constrained devices.

Legacy device risk: Devices with non-updateable firmware or regulatory databases, or devices operating long past their original certification period, may carry regulatory parameters that have been superseded. Regulatory authorities have in some cases changed permitted power levels, introduced listen-before-talk requirements, or restricted previously available frequency ranges. An operator deploying legacy devices with stale RSDGGS databases MUST independently verify that the embedded regulatory parameters remain compliant with current law in the jurisdiction of deployment. This document cannot and does not guarantee the perpetual accuracy of the example band entries in Section 9.

Storage-constrained implementations: Highly constrained devices (Class 0 and Class 1 per RFC 7228, typically less than 10 KB RAM and less than 100 KB flash) may be unable to store complete regulatory databases for all twelve RSDGGS faces. Permissible approaches include: (1) storing only the rule set for the expected operating region (single-face database); (2) storing only the face-level (1-byte) rule set and querying a trusted peer for sub-face details via the bootstrap mechanism in Section 11; (3) storing a minimal safe-mode rule set representing the most restrictive applicable parameters and operating at reduced power until a full database is available. Implementations using approach (1) MUST treat reception of an RSDGGS cell index for an unknown face as a compliance failure requiring the device to cease transmission until it has obtained a valid rule set for that face.

No warranty of compliance: RSDGGS is an informational aid to regulatory self-assessment by constrained IoT devices. Use of a current, accurate RSDGGS database does not constitute a regulatory authorization, does not relieve operators of the obligation to hold any required spectrum licenses, and does not substitute for type approval or certification under the applicable national regulatory framework. Operators remain legally responsible for the compliance of their deployments.

Implementations intended for safety-critical or licensed-spectrum applications SHOULD implement a database version timestamp field and a configurable maximum database age, defaulting to a deployment-class-appropriate value (for example, 365 days for fixed infrastructure, 90 days for mobile equipment). Implementations SHOULD expose the database version and age to management interfaces so that operators can audit fleet-wide database currency.

section.name: 433.05-434.79 MHz (Center: 433.92 MHz)
section.t: This band is designated for ISM use exclusively within ITU Region 1 (Europe, Africa, Middle East, and parts of the former USSR). It is not available as an ISM band in ITU Regions 2 or 3. A single-octet RSDGGS index is sufficient to determine unavailability for all Region 2 and Region 3 faces.

section.name: 863-870 MHz (ETSI SRD Sub-bands)
section.t: This band is the primary short-range device allocation for ITU Region 1 and is governed by ETSI EN 300 220 . It is not available in Regions 2 or 3. The band is internally divided into sub-bands with significantly different duty cycle and power parameters.

section.name: 902-928 MHz (Center: 915 MHz)
section.t: This band is governed primarily by FCC Part 15 Subpart C in the United States and equivalent national regulations in the Americas and selected Asia-Pacific jurisdictions.

This band is the primary sub-GHz ISM allocation for ITU Region 2 and selected Region 3 jurisdictions. It is not available in ITU Region 1 (occupied by GSM-R and other licensed services) or in most of Region 3.

section.name: 920-928 MHz Regional Variants
section.t: The 920-928 MHz band variants are governed by national standards including ARIB STD-T108 in Japan and equivalent regulations in Australia, New Zealand, and other Asia-Pacific jurisdictions.

section.name: TV Whitespace Bands (174-216 MHz, 470-608 MHz)
section.t: TV whitespace bands are available only within the United States (FCC Part 15 Subpart H) and Canada (ISED RSS-222) under Face 2. Unlike static ISM allocations, whitespace channel availability is geofenced and determined dynamically by a regulatory database query at the time of operation.

An RSDGGS cell MUST NOT be used as a static lookup key for whitespace band availability. The RSDGGS index for whitespace-capable devices SHALL be used only to determine whether a whitespace database query is required (RSL 1 sufficient: Face 2 only), and as a location parameter passed to the whitespace database query endpoint. The whitespace database response governs actual channel availability.

section.name: Regulatory Boundary Zones and Adaptive Compliance
section.t: Radio frequency energy does not respect political borders. A device operating lawfully under one regulatory framework may radiate a signal that crosses into a neighboring jurisdiction where the same frequency is prohibited or subject to different power and channelization rules. This section defines how RSDGGS encodes proximity to regulatory boundaries, and how the grid index drives adaptive power control and resolution escalation to ensure that IoT devices operating near such boundaries maintain compliance under both the local and neighboring regulatory frameworks.

section.name: Cross-Border Spectrum Governance Framework
section.t: The international legal framework for managing cross-border spectrum interference operates at four levels, each relevant to the RSDGGS boundary model:

section.name: ITU Radio Regulations
section.t: The ITU Radio Regulations (RR), maintained as a binding international treaty, constitute the supreme global authority for spectrum coordination. Article 15 of the RR specifies procedures for resolving harmful interference between member administrations, requiring administrations to cooperate in detection and elimination. The Master International Frequency Register (MIFR) provides international recognition and interference protection for registered assignments. ITU Radio Regulation footnote 5.150 designates ISM bands globally; footnote 5.138 designates specific bands in specific regions. Footnote 5.280 specifically notes that the 433.05-434.79 MHz band is designated for ISM applications in a named subset of European countries, establishing that this designation is not universal even within ITU Region 1.

For RSDGGS purposes, ITU Region boundaries define the level-0 (single-byte) cell boundaries. Devices at these boundaries encounter the most severe regulatory discontinuities: bands that are legal on one side (e.g., 902-928 MHz in Region 2) are occupied by primary licensed services on the other (GSM-R railways in Region 1). These boundaries are face-edge boundaries in the dodecahedron geometry and are detectable from the face byte of the RSDGGS index.

section.name: Bilateral and Multilateral Coordination Agreements
section.t: Below the ITU level, neighboring administrations negotiate bilateral arrangements governing specific bands along their shared borders. These agreements establish coordination zones — geographic areas on both sides of the border within which proposed assignments require prior approval from the neighboring administration. The zone extent varies by band and agreement:

figure.artwork:
US-Canada (FCC / ISED, per 47 CFR § 1.928 and Arrangements A-Q): Coordination zone: 100-140 km either side of border 800 MHz band zone: 110 km (47 CFR § 90.619) Power limit: ERP and antenna height tables (varies by antenna height above terrain) PFD limit at border: -107 dB(W/m²) for 896-940 MHz
US-Mexico (FCC / IFT, per 47 CFR § 90.619): Sharing zone: 110 km from US/Mexico border 800 MHz primary: Channels divided US/MX primary access PFD limit at border: -107 dB(W/m²) for 896-940 MHz Sub-5W stations: Coordinated only on request
EU internal borders (CEPT/ECC): ETSI EN 300 220 harmonized across EU — no coordination required for intra-EU 868 MHz SRD operation EU/Russia border: coordination required; no harmonization

section.t: The 47 CFR § 90.619 power-flux-density limit of -107 dB(W/m²) at the US/Mexico border for the 896-940 MHz band is directly applicable to ISM-adjacent operations. The 110 km coordination zone for 800 MHz band operations represents a precision requirement of approximately 3-4 bytes of RSDGGS resolution to determine border-zone membership accurately.

section.name: Technical Mitigation Mechanisms
section.t: Within coordination zones, administrations enforce technical constraints to limit signal spillover. These mechanisms have direct analogs in RSDGGS-driven adaptive compliance:

For IoT devices operating under IEEE 802.15.4, directional antenna nulling is generally not available. The primary adaptive mechanism is transmit power reduction, which reduces the effective propagation range and thereby limits the power flux-density at the boundary. RSDGGS provides the geographic trigger for this reduction by computing the distance from the device's current cell to the nearest boundary cell between conflicting rule sets.

section.name: Coordination Zone Geometry and RSDGGS Resolution
section.t: Coordination zone extents established by bilateral agreements map directly to RSDGGS resolution levels. A device must know its position within the applicable coordination zone to apply the correct power limits. The following table maps representative coordination zone radii to the RSDGGS resolution required for unambiguous zone membership determination:

The 3-byte resolution (RSL 3, ~60 km cells) is sufficient to determine whether a device is within the 110-140 km coordination zones established by the FCC-ISED and FCC-IFT bilateral agreements. This aligns with the RSL values defined in Section 8.2 for most regulatory jurisdictions. For the innermost protection zones (e.g., the 30 km London, Ontario zone in the FCC-ISED 700 MHz arrangement), 4-byte resolution is required. Maritime territorial sea boundaries require 5-byte resolution.

section.name: Boundary Proximity Function
section.t: RSDGGS defines a boundary proximity function B(cell, band) that returns the distance in RSDGGS resolution steps between a given cell and the nearest cell boundary at which the applicable rule set for the specified band changes. The function is evaluated against the regulatory database exception table (Section 8.3) and the bilateral coordination zone table.

figure.artwork:
B(cell, band): Input: cell — RSDGGS cell index at current resolution R band — ISM band identifier Output: steps — number of subdivision levels to nearest rule-set-changing boundary 0 = boundary within current cell 1 = boundary in adjacent cell at level R N = boundary N levels away
If B(cell, band) == 0: Current cell straddles a regulatory boundary. Device MUST increase resolution until B > 0, or apply the more restrictive of the two rule sets.
If B(cell, band) <= THRESHOLD_STEPS: Device is in a coordination zone. Apply boundary_power_profile(cell, band, B).
If B(cell, band) > THRESHOLD_STEPS: Device is not in a coordination zone. Apply standard rule set for current cell.
Recommended THRESHOLD_STEPS by coordination zone: ITU Region face boundary: B <= 2 (face-edge cells) 110-140 km bilateral zone: B <= 3 (3-byte resolution) 30 km protection zone: B <= 4 (4-byte resolution) 12 nm territorial sea: B <= 5 (5-byte resolution)

section.name: Adaptive Power Control at Regulatory Boundaries
section.t: When a device determines that B(cell, band) <= THRESHOLD_STEPS, it enters boundary-aware operation and applies a graduated power reduction profile. The profile scales transmit power based on the proximity function value, reducing power as the device approaches the boundary such that the power flux-density at the boundary line remains below the applicable coordination threshold.

section.name: Power Reduction Profile
section.t: The transmitted power at proximity step B is:

figure.artwork:
P_tx(B) = min(P_max_local, P_max_neighbor) - G(B)
Where: P_max_local = maximum EIRP permitted by local rule set P_max_neighbor = maximum EIRP permitted by neighboring rule set G(B) = graduated reduction factor by proximity step
Recommended G(B) values: B >= THRESHOLD: G = 0 dB (no reduction, interior operation) B = 3: G = 3 dB (half power; outer coordination zone) B = 2: G = 6 dB (quarter power; inner zone) B = 1: G = 10 dB (1/10 power; adjacent to boundary) B = 0: G = P_max_local - P_max_neighbor (take minimum of both rule sets)
The G(B) values above are RECOMMENDED defaults. Implementations MAY substitute a continuous function: G(d) = 20 * log10(d_0 / d) dB where d is the estimated distance to the boundary in meters and d_0 is the coordination zone radius in meters. This continuous form requires 5-byte resolution to evaluate with adequate precision (cell diameter ~1 km).

section.t: The minimum neighbor power constraint (taking the minimum of the two rule sets at B=0) is the most conservative applicable interpretation of cross-border coordination obligations. It corresponds to the principle that a device straddling a boundary cannot claim the more permissive of two jurisdictions and must comply with both simultaneously.

section.name: Duty Cycle and Dwell Constraints
section.t: In addition to power reduction, boundary-aware operation applies the more restrictive duty cycle and dwell constraints of the two adjacent rule sets. This is particularly significant at EU/non-EU boundaries where the ETSI 868 MHz sub-band duty cycle limits (0.1% to 10%) differ materially from non-EU frameworks that may impose no duty cycle constraint.

figure.artwork:
At B = 0 (boundary cell), apply: duty_cycle = min(DC_local, DC_neighbor) dwell_s = min(dwell_local, dwell_neighbor) lbt = local_lbt OR neighbor_lbt
Example: EU/Russia border, 868 MHz band EU: duty_cycle = 1%, lbt = false (EN 300 220) Russia: duty_cycle = none, lbt = false (GOST-R) → Apply DC = 1%, lbt = false
Example: EU/Switzerland border, 868 MHz band EU: ETSI EN 300 220 in full Switzerland: ETSI-aligned (OFCOM, independent) → Effectively identical, no reduction needed → Exception table entry flags as RSL 5 for verification

section.name: RSDGGS Resolution Escalation Near Boundaries
section.t: The closer a device is to a regulatory boundary, the finer the resolution required to accurately determine its position relative to that boundary. RSDGGS defines a resolution escalation requirement: the device MUST maintain a RSDGGS index at a resolution sufficient to resolve its boundary proximity function to at least one non-zero value.

figure.artwork:
Resolution escalation rule:
If current_resolution < RSL(face, band): Increase resolution to RSL(face, band).
If B(cell, band) == 0 at current_resolution: // Boundary is within current cell — ambiguous Increase resolution by one byte. Re-evaluate B(cell, band). Repeat until B > 0 or resolution == 8 bytes.
If resolution == 8 bytes and B == 0: // Device is within ~3 cm of the boundary line // (sub-decimeter precision — effectively on the line) Apply conservative rule: use minimum of both rule sets. Log condition for operator review.
Maximum practical resolution for boundary determination: 5 bytes (~1 km) — adequate for bilateral zone classification 6 bytes (~120 m) — adequate for most land borders 7 bytes (~15 m) — adequate for all practical land borders

section.t: The resolution escalation requirement means that a device moving toward a regulatory boundary will autonomously increase its index precision as it approaches, consuming more power in the cooperative localization process (Section 12) but ensuring that its compliance determination remains accurate. For fixed devices, this escalation occurs once at commissioning and the resulting high-resolution index is stored permanently.

The escalation is bounded: for the vast majority of IoT deployments, 3-byte resolution is sufficient for all regulatory decisions and boundary detection. Resolution escalation beyond 5 bytes is only required for devices within approximately 1 km of a land border between jurisdictions with conflicting ISM band rules — a scenario that affects only a small fraction of deployed devices.

section.name: CDDL Schema for Boundary-Aware Operation
section.t: The following CDDL extensions define the data structures for boundary-aware operation:

figure.artwork:
boundary-context = { cell: rsdggs-cell, ; cell at escalated resolution B: uint, ; boundary proximity steps rule-local: uint, ; rule set ID for current cell rule-neighbor: nil / uint, ; rule set ID of nearest neighbor ; nil if B > THRESHOLD p-tx-dbm: int, ; applied TX power in dBm p-reduction-db: uint, ; dB reduction from P_max_local dc-applied: nil / float, ; applied duty cycle fraction lbt-required: bool, ; LBT enforced }
boundary-entry = { ; in regulatory database cell-a: rsdggs-cell, ; cell on one side of boundary cell-b: rsdggs-cell, ; cell on other side band-id: uint, agreement: tstr, ; treaty/agreement citation zone-km: uint, ; coordination zone radius in km pfd-limit-dbwm2: int, ; PFD limit at boundary dB(W/m²) p-max-a-dbm: int, ; max EIRP in cell-a p-max-b-dbm: int, ; max EIRP in cell-b dc-a: nil / float, ; duty cycle in cell-a dc-b: nil / float, ; duty cycle in cell-b }

section.t: The boundary-entry table in the regulatory database is indexed by the pair (cell-a, cell-b) at the finest resolution at which the two cells are adjacent cells. For face-edge boundaries (ITU Region boundaries), the index is at byte 0 (face only). For bilateral coordination zone boundaries, the index is at bytes 3-4. For land border crossing point exceptions, the index may be at bytes 5-6.

The boundary-entry pfd-limit-dbwm2 field enables a device with knowledge of its antenna characteristics and propagation environment to compute the maximum transmit power that keeps its signal below the applicable PFD limit at the boundary. For IoT devices using typical isotropic or near-isotropic antennas, a simplified free-space path loss model is sufficient for this computation. Implementations SHOULD implement the free-space PFD computation as a compile-time table indexed by (distance-to-boundary-km, P_tx-dBm) to avoid floating-point computation on constrained devices.

section.name: Peer-Assisted Location Discovery
section.t: Many IoT devices lack GPS receivers or smartphone tethering and have no independent means of determining their geographic location. In conformance with design goal G8 (Section 3), RSDGGS is designed so that a device with no external connectivity — no DHCP server, no DNS, no cloud enrollment, no smartphone tether — SHALL be capable of full regulatory self-configuration through peer interaction alone. RSDGGS defines a peer-assisted discovery mechanism enabling such Naive Devices to derive their applicable regulatory parameters from beacons transmitted by location-aware Beacon Devices in the vicinity. This mechanism is the primary regulatory bootstrap path, not a fallback: centralized provisioning systems such as DHCP servers are optional accelerators, not dependencies.

section.name: Beacon Frame Format
section.t: A Beacon Device that has resolved its regulatory context SHALL periodically transmit a beacon frame on its active ISM channel. The beacon frame is encoded as a CBOR map and MUST include the beacon-frame structure defined in Section 7.3. The RSDGGS cell in the beacon frame SHALL be encoded at no greater than RSL depth for the band in use, as a privacy measure for the Beacon Device.

The transmitted RSDGGS cell inherently encodes which ISM channels are legal at the Beacon Device's location, since the Beacon Device, by definition, is transmitting on a legal channel for its jurisdiction. A Naive Device receiving the beacon on that channel can infer that the channel is legal at the Beacon Device's location. If the Naive Device is in the same RSDGGS cell as the Beacon Device at RSL depth, it MAY apply the same rule set.

section.name: Manufacturing Provisioning Use Case
section.t: RSDGGS enables a single global hardware SKU to be provisioned with location-specific regulatory parameters at manufacturing time, eliminating the need for hardware or firmware variants differentiated by target market. Pre-provisioning at manufacturing time is one of three equally valid provisioning paths; the others are peer-assisted bootstrap (Section 11) and tethered-device provisioning (Section 11.3). In all three cases, the provisioned RSDGGS cell is stored in non-volatile device memory and does not require ongoing connectivity to any server to be applied.

This section does not preclude optional use of infrastructure-based provisioning mechanisms such as DHCPv6 (analogous to RFC 3825, which defines a DHCP option for geodetic coordinates) or cloud enrollment APIs using device authorization flows such as those defined in . However, in conformance with design goal G8, infrastructure-based provisioning MUST NOT be the only path to regulatory compliance. section.name: Cooperative Localization
section.t: A Naive Device that has no independent means of determining its geographic location MAY infer its position through cooperative localization: a process by which the device aggregates RSDGGS cell assertions, signal strength measurements, and precision ranging measurements from multiple peers to derive a position estimate expressed as an RSDGGS cell at the finest resolution consistent with the accumulated measurement uncertainty.

This section defines the localization method hierarchy, the procedures for each method, the RSDGGS-native position state space, and the integration of these methods into a unified estimation engine. IEEE 802.15.4a HRP UWB ranging and IEEE 802.15.4z enhanced ranging are defined as the highest-precision input to the estimation engine and are treated in detail.

section.name: Localization Method Hierarchy
section.t: Three localization methods are defined, ordered from coarsest to finest achievable precision. The methods are composable: a device SHOULD apply all available methods simultaneously, using each as a weighted input to the unified estimation engine defined in Section 11.6.

A device with access only to Method M1 can resolve its RSDGGS cell to the intersection of its peers' cells, typically 2–4 bytes of resolution. A device with M2 capability can typically achieve 6-byte resolution (120 m) in outdoor environments. A device with M3 capability can achieve 7–8 byte resolution (2–15 m) in line-of-sight conditions.

section.name: RSDGGS Cell Intersection
section.t: Each beacon received from a peer carries an RSDGGS cell at the RSL depth for the transmitting channel. The Naive Device accumulates received cells and maintains the geographic intersection of all received cells as a constraint on its own position.

The intersection of two RSDGGS cells is defined as the longest common prefix of their bit representations. If two cells share a common prefix of length L bits, then any point within both cells must lie within the geographic region represented by that L-bit prefix. The intersection cell is that prefix, truncated to the nearest byte boundary.

figure.artwork:
Cell intersection algorithm:
received_cells: list of (cell_bytes, peer_id) intersection: uint64_t initialized to 0 valid_bits: uint = 64
for each (cell, peer) in received_cells: cell_u64 = cell padded to 8 bytes (zero-extended) xor = intersection XOR cell_u64 // find highest differing bit diff_bit = 64 - clz(xor) // clz = count leading zeros if diff_bit < valid_bits: valid_bits = diff_bit intersection = cell_u64 & ~((1 << diff_bit) - 1)
resolution_bytes = valid_bits / 8 // floor inferred_cell = intersection >> (64 - resolution_bytes*8)

section.t: As additional peers are heard, valid_bits can only decrease or remain constant, monotonically converging toward the finest common prefix. When peers at higher resolution (more bytes) are heard, the intersection tightens. A Naive Device SHOULD advertise its inferred cell at the current resolution once it has received cells from at least three peers, to assist other Naive Devices in the vicinity.

section.name: Round-Trip RSSI Range Estimation
section.t: RSSI-based range estimation uses the log-distance path loss model to convert measured signal strength to a distance estimate. The round-trip exchange eliminates first-order asymmetric fading bias by averaging path loss in both directions.

figure.artwork: Initiator A Responder B | | |-- Data(cell_A, req_rssi) -->>| RSSI_B_rx = RSSI of frame at B | | |<<--- Enhanced ACK(RSSI_B_rx) -------| RSSI_A_rx = RSSI of ACK at A | | |-- RSSI Report(RSSI_A_rx) -------->>| | | Both nodes now hold (RSSI_B_rx, RSSI_A_rx) Path loss = (RSSI_tx_A - RSSI_B_rx + RSSI_tx_B - RSSI_A_rx) / 2

section.name: Range Estimation
section.t: The range estimate from bidirectional path loss is computed using the log-distance model. Path loss exponent n and reference path loss PL(d0) at reference distance d0 are environmental parameters stored in device configuration.

figure.artwork:
PL = (TX_power_A - RSSI_B_rx + TX_power_B - RSSI_A_rx) / 2 [dB]
Range estimate: d = d0 * 10 ^ ((PL_measured - PL(d0)) / (10 * n)) [meters]
Range uncertainty (1-sigma): sigma_d = (ln(10) / (10*n)) * d * sigma_PL
sigma_PL: shadowing standard deviation, typically 4-8 dB
Recommended defaults (absent site survey): d0 = 1.0 m PL(d0)= 40.0 dB (2.4 GHz free space at 1 m) n = 2.7 (light indoor / suburban) sigma = 6.0 dB

section.t: The range estimate d and uncertainty sigma_d from each peer constitute one range measurement for input to the multilateration engine in Section 11.6. Multiple round-trip exchanges with the same peer SHOULD be averaged to reduce the contribution of sigma_PL. The minimum recommended number of exchanges per peer before using the range in multilateration is three.

section.name: IEEE 802.15.4a/z UWB Precision Ranging
section.t: IEEE 802.15.4a defines the High-Rate Pulse (HRP) UWB physical layer and the ranging primitives used to achieve centimeter-class range measurements. IEEE 802.15.4z augments these with the Scrambled Timestamp Sequence (STS) for cryptographic binding of timestamps to a shared session key, preventing range manipulation by adversarial nodes.

section.name: Double-Sided Two-Way Ranging (DS-TWR)
section.t: Double-Sided Two-Way Ranging eliminates the first-order clock offset bias present in Single-Sided TWR. It requires three messages: Poll, Response, and Final, with optional Report for enhanced bias cancellation.

figure.artwork:
Initiator A Responder B | | |== Poll (SP1/SP3, STS) =============>>| t1(A), t2(B) | | |<<= Response (SP1/SP3, STS) =========| t3(B), t4(A) | | |== Final (SP1/SP3, STS) =============>>| t5(A), t6(B) | | |<<= Report (optional) ===============| B sends t2,t3,t6 to A | |
Single-sided ToF (A's perspective): ToF_A = ((t4 - t1) - (t3 - t2)) / 2
Double-sided ToF (eliminates clock offset): ToF = ((t4-t1)(t6-t3) - (t3-t2)(t5-t4)) / (2 * ((t4-t1) + (t6-t3)))
Range = ToF * c (c = 299,792,458 m/s)
Typical precision: +/- 10 cm LoS, +/- 30-50 cm NLoS

section.name: STS Authentication (802.15.4z)
section.t: The Scrambled Timestamp Sequence (STS) field, defined in IEEE 802.15.4z, is a pseudorandom sequence generated from a shared session key known only to legitimate peers. The STS is embedded in the UWB pulse train immediately before the ranging timestamp. A receiver can authenticate that the timestamp was generated by a node holding the shared key, preventing a malicious node from injecting false timestamps to manipulate range estimates.

Implementations using cooperative localization for regulatory compliance MUST use SP1 or SP3 packet formats with STS enabled when UWB ranging is available. The STS session key SHALL be derived from the network join credentials established during PAN association, ensuring that only authenticated PAN members can contribute ranging measurements to the localization engine.

Implementations MUST reject ranging measurements from peers that fail STS authentication. A pattern of STS authentication failures from a specific peer SHOULD be reported to the application layer as a potential ranging attack.

section.name: Phase Difference of Arrival (PDOA) Angle Estimation
section.t: Devices equipped with two or more UWB antennas separated by a known baseline d_ant MAY compute the angle of arrival of a UWB signal using the phase difference between antennas. The angle estimate provides a directional constraint that supplements the scalar range measurement.

figure.artwork:
PDOA angle estimation:
delta_phi: measured phase difference between antennas [radians] d_ant: antenna separation [meters] lambda: UWB center wavelength [meters]
theta = arcsin(delta_phi * lambda / (2 * pi * d_ant)) [radians]
Uncertainty: sigma_theta = sigma_phi * lambda / (2 * pi * d_ant * cos(theta))
Typical: +/- 5 degrees at 50 cm baseline, +/- 2 degrees at 1.25 m

section.t: The PDOA angle theta and uncertainty sigma_theta from each UWB-capable peer constitute an angular measurement for input to the multilateration engine. The combination of DS-TWR range and PDOA angle from a single peer provides a 2D position fix relative to that peer, without requiring a second ranging peer.

section.name: RSDGGS as Position State Space
section.t: Rather than maintaining a floating-point latitude/longitude position estimate, the cooperative localization engine represents position state natively as an RSDGGS cell index at the finest resolution consistent with the current position uncertainty. This representation is exact within the quantization of the cell size, requires no floating-point arithmetic at the application layer, and directly produces the regulatory cell needed for ISM band validation.

The position uncertainty is maintained as a single integer sigma_cells, representing the radius of the position uncertainty ellipse in units of RSDGGS cells at the current resolution. When sigma_cells falls below 1 at the current resolution, the resolution is incremented (one byte added) and sigma_cells is recomputed in terms of the finer cells. When sigma_cells grows beyond a threshold (RECOMMENDED: 4 cells), the resolution is decremented (one byte removed).

This adaptive quantization ensures that the RSDGGS cell always represents the region within which the device's true position lies with high probability, without overstating precision. A device reporting its cell at 3-byte resolution is asserting that its position is within the corresponding 60 km cell; a device reporting at 7-byte resolution is asserting position within 15 m.

section.name: Weighted Multilateration Engine
section.t: The multilateration engine fuses M1 (cell intersection), M2 (RSSI range), and M3 (UWB range and angle) measurements into a unified position estimate in RSDGGS space. The engine operates iteratively, updating the position state each time a new measurement arrives.

section.name: Measurement Model
section.t: Each peer P_i contributes one or more of the following measurements:

section.name: Weighted Least Squares Position Update
section.t: Given ranges {r_i} or {R_i} to N peers at known cells {C_i}, the position update minimizes the weighted sum of squared residuals:

figure.artwork:
Minimize: sum_i ( w_i * (d(pos, C_i_center) - r_i)^2 )
w_i = 1 / sigma_i^2 (RSSI) or 1 / epsilon_i^2 (UWB) d(.,.) = great-circle distance between RSDGGS cell centers
Cell center of an RSDGGS cell: Midpoint of the bounding isosceles triangle at that resolution, computed from the triangle vertex positions on the unit sphere.
Minimum peers required for 2D fix: M1 only: 3 peers (for non-degenerate intersection) M2 (RSSI range only): 3 peers (trilateration) M3 (UWB range only): 2 peers (+ PDOA) or 3 peers (range only) M3 (range + PDOA): 1 peer (2D fix relative to peer)

section.t: For constrained devices, a closed-form linearized solution is RECOMMENDED over iterative nonlinear solvers. The linearization uses the current position estimate as the operating point and applies a first-order Taylor expansion of the range function, reducing the problem to a linear least squares system solvable by the normal equations. This requires only integer arithmetic in RSDGGS cell units and is implementable on Cortex-M0 class devices.

section.name: Extended Kalman Filter Integration
section.t: For mobile devices, the multilateration engine is augmented with a discrete-time Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) that propagates the position estimate through time using a motion model and updates it with incoming measurements.

figure.artwork:
State vector x = [cell_index, velocity_cells_per_sec, sigma_cells]
cell_index: uint64_t, RSDGGS cell at current resolution velocity: signed integer, cells/second at resolution zero for fixed devices sigma_cells: uint16_t, position uncertainty radius in cells

Prediction (between measurements, interval dt seconds):
x_pred = x + velocity * dt [cell index advance] P_pred = P + Q * dt [covariance propagation]
Q: process noise covariance Fixed device: Q = 0 (no motion expected) Pedestrian: Q corresponds to ~1.5 m/s max velocity Vehicle: Q corresponds to ~30 m/s max velocity
Cell adjacency graph used for index advance: neighbor cell in direction of velocity vector derived from dodecahedron subdivision adjacency

section.name: Update Step
section.t: Each incoming measurement (RSSI range, UWB range, PDOA angle, or cell assertion) constitutes a Kalman update. The measurement Jacobian H maps from the state vector to the expected measurement, evaluated at the current predicted state. The Kalman gain weights the measurement relative to the predicted state uncertainty.

Cell assertions from Method M1 are incorporated as a hard constraint: if the current predicted position cell is inconsistent with the received peer cell, the position state is reset to the intersection cell and the uncertainty sigma_cells is set to reflect the intersection cell size. This prevents the EKF from drifting outside the hard geographic bounds established by peer cell assertions.

For fixed devices, the EKF reduces to a static estimator. The prediction step adds no uncertainty (Q = 0) and successive measurements monotonically reduce sigma_cells until the RSDGGS resolution stabilizes at 7–8 bytes for UWB-capable deployments, or 5–6 bytes for RSSI-only deployments.

section.name: Security Considerations for Cooperative Ranging
section.t: Cooperative localization introduces attack surfaces that are not present in GPS-based positioning or static provisioning. An adversarial node could transmit false RSDGGS cells, false RSSI values, or manipulated UWB timestamps to induce a Naive Device to believe it is in a different regulatory jurisdiction, potentially causing it to operate on illegal channels.

Cell Assertion Spoofing: A malicious peer could broadcast a false RSDGGS cell, causing the Naive Device to adopt an incorrect regulatory rule set. Mitigation: require cell assertions from a minimum of three independent peers before adopting a regulatory context (Section 10.3). Cells from multiple independent peers that are mutually consistent are significantly harder to spoof collectively.

RSSI Manipulation: A high-power transmitter could present an artificially strong RSSI, causing the localization engine to place the Naive Device's position erroneously close to the adversary. Mitigation: apply a maximum plausible range gradient filter; discard measurements where round-trip RSSI implies an implausibly large or small range given the known transmit power.

UWB Timestamp Manipulation: Without STS authentication, a malicious node could inject false timestamps in the DS-TWR exchange, inducing a false range measurement. Mitigation: use STS-authenticated ranging (SP1 or SP3 packet formats) as REQUIRED in Section 11.4.2. Discard all UWB range measurements from peers that fail STS authentication.

Regulatory Boundary Induction: A coordinated attack by multiple adversarial nodes could attempt to place a Naive Device's inferred cell at a regulatory boundary, inducing the device to apply an incorrect rule set. Mitigation: when the inferred cell straddles a regulatory boundary (as indicated by the exception flag in the regulatory database), require UWB-authenticated ranging to at least one peer before committing to a regulatory context.

section.name: IE Structure and Constraints
section.t: IEEE 802.15.4-2020 defines two classes of Information Elements (IEs) that may be included in MAC frames. Header IEs carry type 0 with IDs in the range 0x00 to 0x7E and a maximum payload of 127 octets. Payload IEs carry type 1 with Group IDs in the range 0x00 to 0x0F and a maximum payload of 2047 octets. Payload IEs may contain nested Sub-IEs.

The MLME Payload IE (Group ID 0x01) is the standard container for MAC-layer management sub-elements including the SUN (Smart Utility Network) Device Description Sub-IEs defined in IEEE 802.15.4g and extended in IEEE 802.15.4-2020 Section 7.4. RSDGGS location information is carried as a new Sub-IE nested within this container.
The Sub-IE header structure is two octets:

figure.artwork:
Sub-IE Header (2 octets): Bits [15:8] Sub-IE ID (8 bits) — assigned by IEEE RA Bits [7:0] Length (8 bits) — payload length in octets
Sub-IE Payload (1-8 octets): RSDGGS cell bytes, variable length
The Length field value equals the number of RSDGGS cell octets and therefore directly encodes the spatial resolution of the index, consistent with the CBOR encoding defined in Section 7.

section.name: RSDGGS Location Sub-IE Definition
section.t: The RSDGGS Location Sub-IE is defined as follows. The Sub-IE ID value is pending assignment by the IEEE Registration Authority. The placeholder value 0x9A is used in this document.

A receiver MUST interpret the Length field as the RSDGGS resolution level. A Length of 1 indicates face-only resolution. A Length of 0 is invalid and MUST be rejected. A Length greater than 8 is invalid and MUST be rejected. Reserved face values (0x0C to 0x0F in Cell[0]) MUST be treated as an error condition.

The Sub-IE MAY appear in any MAC frame type that permits Payload IEs, including Beacon frames, Enhanced Beacon frames, Data frames, and Command frames. It SHALL appear in the SUN Device Description payload of Enhanced Beacon frames transmitted by devices that have resolved their regulatory context.

section.name: SUN Device Description Integration
section.t: The SUN Device Description IE (Sub-IE ID 0x08 within the MLME Payload IE group) is transmitted by SUN devices during PAN formation and association to advertise device capabilities. The RSDGGS Location Sub-IE SHALL be included in the SUN Device Description payload of any device that has resolved its regulatory context.

The resolution at which the RSDGGS cell is encoded in the Sub-IE SHALL be the Resolution Sufficiency Level (RSL) for the ISM band on which the frame is transmitted, as defined in Section 8.2. This ensures that the regulatory cell carried in the IE is sufficient for a receiving device to determine the applicable rule set, while not disclosing more precise location than required for regulatory purposes.

The Sub-IE Length field thus serves three simultaneous functions: it specifies the IE payload length as required by the 802.15.4 framing specification; it encodes the RSDGGS resolution level implicitly; and it signals the privacy posture of the transmitting device (a shorter cell = coarser location = more privacy-preserving).

figure.artwork: Enhanced Beacon Frame (abbreviated): MHR Payload IE: Group ID = 0x01 (MLME) Sub-IE: ID = 0x08 (SUN Device Description) ... capability fields ... Sub-IE: ID = 0x9A (RSDGGS Location) Length = 0x03 (3 octets, country-level RSL) Cell = 0x02 0xA4 0x30 ^^^^ face 2 = ITU Region 2 / N. America ^^^^ ^^^^ subdivision to ~60 km cell MFR
