section.t: The inclusion of RSDGGS location in the SUN Device Description enables regulatory bootstrap at the MAC layer, prior to any application stack initialization. The procedure is as follows:

This MAC-layer integration enables fully automated regulatory provisioning during PAN formation, with no application-layer involvement. A device joining a well-managed SUN PAN will have its regulatory context resolved as a side effect of the standard association procedure.

section.name: IPv6 Geographic Addressing
section.t: The full 8-octet RSDGGS index fits precisely within the 64-bit Interface Identifier (IID) field of an IPv6 address. This alignment enables a class of IPv6 addresses in which the IID encodes a geographic cell rather than a hardware identifier, enabling geographic routing without a routing table.

section.name: Address Structure
section.t: An RSDGGS Geographic IPv6 address is structured as follows:

The upper 64 bits form the network prefix, which identifies the address as belonging to the RSDGGS geographic address space. This prefix is to be assigned from the IANA Special-Purpose Address Registry for use with this specification. The placeholder prefix GEO::/64 is used in this document pending IANA assignment.

The lower 64 bits are the RSDGGS cell index in the 8-octet encoding defined in Section 5, with the most significant byte (Octet 0, the face byte) placed in the most significant octet of the IID. Unused subdivision bits in the terminal resolution level are set to zero.

The address is self-describing at any prefix length: the geographic region corresponding to a /N prefix is the set of RSDGGS cells sharing the same upper N bits of their IID. This is directly equivalent to RSDGGS index truncation at the corresponding resolution level.

section.name: Prefix Hierarchy and Aggregation
section.t: The RSDGGS hierarchical structure maps directly onto IPv6 prefix aggregation. The following prefix lengths correspond to RSDGGS resolution levels:

A /72 prefix encompasses all devices in a single ITU Region. A /88 prefix encompasses all devices within a single country-scale cell. This aggregation is lossless: any RSDGGS cell address is aggregatable at any of the above prefix boundaries without loss of hierarchical information.

Routing tables for geographic address spaces can therefore aggregate aggressively. A continental backbone router needs only /72 or /80 routes. A national backbone router needs only /88 routes. A metropolitan router needs only /96 routes. Leaf-level routing to specific devices uses the full /128.

section.name: Geographic Greedy Forwarding
section.t: A forwarder holding an RSDGGS Geographic IPv6 address for itself and receiving a packet destined for another geographic address can make a forwarding decision purely from address arithmetic, without a routing table.

figure.artwork:
Forwarding algorithm:
G_self = local RSDGGS cell (from own address IID) G_dest = destination RSDGGS cell (from packet dest IID) G_next = next-hop RSDGGS cell (from neighbor table)
common_prefix_len(A, B): count of matching most-significant bits in IID of A and B
progress(A, B, target): common_prefix_len(A, target) > common_prefix_len(B, target)
For each candidate next hop N in neighbor table: if progress(G_next[N], G_self, G_dest): forward to N // N is geographically closer to destination
If no progress possible: invoke void handling (perimeter routing or buffer-and-wait)

section.t: The progress metric is purely a comparison of common prefix lengths. No trigonometric computation is required at forwarding time. The geographic distance relationship is encoded in the shared prefix structure of the RSDGGS hierarchy: a longer common prefix means a smaller shared cell means geographic proximity.

This forwarding algorithm is equivalent to greedy geographic forwarding as used in GPSR and similar protocols, but operates on the RSDGGS index structure directly rather than on Euclidean or great-circle distance. The computational cost at each hop is a bitwise XOR and leading-zero count — operations available as single instructions on all target architectures including constrained microcontrollers.

section.name: Regulatory-Aware Channel Selection for Forwarding
section.t: The geographic address carries implicit regulatory information through the face byte of the IID. A forwarder can extract the face byte of the destination address to determine the ITU Region of the destination, and therefore the ISM band availability at the destination.

When a packet is forwarded toward a destination in a different regulatory cell, the forwarding node SHOULD select a transmission channel that is legal in both its own regulatory cell and the next-hop's regulatory cell. If no such channel exists (for example, forwarding from an EU 868 MHz network toward a US 915 MHz network), the forwarder MUST NOT transmit on a channel that is illegal in either jurisdiction.

In practice, cross-regulatory-region forwarding at the ISM layer requires either a gateway device provisioned for both regulatory environments, or an application-layer relay. The geographic address structure makes this boundary explicit and machine-readable: a mismatch in the face byte of the IID between source and destination indicates a cross-regulatory-region path that requires special handling.

section.name: Relationship to Existing Standards
section.t: The RSDGGS Geographic IPv6 addressing scheme intersects with the following existing standards and efforts, from which it draws and to which it contributes:

RFC 4944 / RFC 6282 (6LoWPAN): The IID derivation from EUI-64 defined in RFC 4944 is not applicable to geographic addresses. Implementations using RSDGGS Geographic addressing over 802.15.4 SHALL use the RSDGGS cell as the IID directly and MUST NOT apply the EUI-64 IID derivation procedure. The 6LoWPAN header compression schemes defined in RFC 6282 are applicable to geographic addresses with the understanding that the IID carries geographic rather than hardware identity.

RFC 6775 (6LoWPAN-ND): The Neighbor Discovery optimization defined in RFC 6775 for low-power networks applies to geographic addresses. The geographic IID provides a natural mechanism for duplicate address detection in dense deployments: two devices with the same geographic cell at maximum resolution are, by definition, co-located within approximately 3 centimeters and may legitimately share an address for aggregated sensing applications.

RFC 9854 (AODV-RPL): Geographic greedy forwarding as defined in Section 13.3 eliminates the need for route discovery in dense geographic deployments. AODV-RPL route discovery MAY be used as a fallback void-handling mechanism when greedy forwarding cannot make progress, for example in sparse networks with geographic holes. The RSDGGS cell can serve as the position metric in AODV-RPL's P2P route discovery in place of GPS coordinates, enabling route discovery on devices without GPS receivers.

ETSI EN 302 931 (GeoNetworking): The European ITS GeoNetworking standard defines geographic addressing over 802.11p and LTE for vehicular networks. RSDGGS Geographic IPv6 addressing is an alternative approach designed for low-power ISM-band IoT networks rather than vehicular ITS, with the additional property of encoding regulatory jurisdiction within the address structure.

IEEE 802.15.4 SUN: The MAC-layer integration defined in Section 12 and the IPv6 geographic addressing defined in this section are complementary. A SUN network using RSDGGS Location Sub-IEs at the MAC layer and RSDGGS Geographic IPv6 addresses at the network layer achieves end-to-end geographic addressing from the MAC frame through the IP datagram, with regulatory context embedded at both layers.

section.name: Relationship to Prior Geographic Addressing Work
section.t: Several IETF documents address geographic location representation, conveyance, and routing. This section compares each to RSDGGS, identifying the gaps that RSDGGS addresses and the areas where these prior works remain authoritative and complementary.

The fundamental distinction between RSDGGS and all prior work is axis of design: the existing RFCs treat geographic location as a property to be conveyed alongside an application or network protocol, using coordinate systems (WGS-84 latitude/longitude) designed for human-readable precision. RSDGGS treats geographic location as a self-describing, hierarchical index whose structure directly encodes regulatory jurisdiction, enables address-arithmetic routing, and is optimized for constrained IoT devices operating without floating-point arithmetic or external infrastructure.

section.name: RFC 2009: GPS-Based Addressing and Routing
section.t: RFC 2009 (Imielinski and Navas, 1996) is the earliest IETF treatment of geographic addressing and routing. It is categorized as Experimental and carries Legacy status, meaning it was published before formal source tracking and has no standing in the IETF standards process. Despite its age, it establishes several concepts directly relevant to RSDGGS.

section.name: RFC 2009 Technical Approach
section.t: RFC 2009 proposes extending IP routing to support geographic destination addressing using GPS coordinates. The core concept is the Geographic Service Area: each router is assigned a bounding polygon defined in GPS coordinates (latitude/longitude pairs) representing the geographic region it serves. A new protocol, IGPSMP (Internet GPS Management Protocol), allows routers to exchange service area descriptions using six message types: set-service-area, confirm-service-area, geographic-service-area-query, service-area-report, and related management primitives.

For indoor environments where GPS is unavailable, RFC 2009 proposes weak radio beacons that broadcast a GPS address, allowing mobile devices to adopt the beacon's address as their own. This is structurally analogous to the peer-assisted discovery mechanism defined in Section 10 of this document.

RFC 2009 also proposes a DNS-based application-layer solution, adding a geographic first-level domain with hierarchical sub-domains for states, counties, and polygons of interest. Routing to a geographic address involves translating the destination polygon into a sequence of router hops based on IGPSMP service area tables.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 2009 RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Coordinate system WGS-84 lat/lon polys Dodecahedral cell index Wire encoding Float-point GPS coord 1-8 byte int (uint64_t) Constrained devices Not considered no_std, no_alloc, no FPU Routing metric Polygon intersection Prefix len (XOR+CLZ) Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Indoor location Beacon GPS addr copy Cell + UWB ranging Privacy Not addressed Truncation gradient Status Experimental / Legacy Informational (this doc)

section.t: RFC 2009's polygon-based service areas require floating-point computation for containment tests and polygon intersection, making them unsuitable for the Cortex-M0 class devices that constitute the majority of 802.15.4 IoT deployments. The IGPSMP protocol requires routers to maintain geographic routing tables that grow with network size, whereas RSDGGS geographic addressing enables stateless forwarding decisions from address arithmetic alone.

RFC 2009 does not address regulatory spectrum management, band availability, or the use of geographic addressing to encode regulatory jurisdiction. RSDGGS is the first specification to treat these as primary design goals of a geographic addressing system.

section.name: RFC 5870: The 'geo' URI Scheme
section.t: RFC 5870 (Mayrhofer and Spanring, 2010) defines the 'geo' URI scheme for identifying geographic locations in a coordinate reference system. It is a Standards Track document. The scheme is widely deployed in web contexts, QR codes, mapping applications, and messaging systems.

section.name: RFC 5870 Technical Approach
section.t: A 'geo' URI encodes a point location in WGS-84 (default) or an alternative CRS using the syntax geo:lat,lon[,alt][;crs=...][;u=uncertainty]. The coordinate values are decimal degrees (latitude and longitude) with optional altitude in meters. An optional uncertainty parameter u= specifies the radius of the location in meters. The number of decimal digits in the coordinate values MUST NOT be interpreted as an indication of accuracy; uncertainty is carried only in the explicit u= parameter.

The scheme is CRS-agnostic: while WGS-84 is the default, alternative coordinate reference systems may be specified using the crs= parameter. The scheme is protocol-independent and may appear in any context supporting arbitrary URIs.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 5870 'geo' URI RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Representation 'geo:48.2,16.4;u=40' Binary: 0x02 0xA4 0x30 Encoding size 20-30 bytes typical 1-8 bytes Uncertainty Float param (u=) Implicit in byte length Privacy control Digit trunc (lossy) Byte trunc (lossless) Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Routing use Not defined See Section 13 Constrained devices Text parsing required Integer extraction only Hierarchical index None Full hier. in bits

section.t: RFC 5870 explicitly states that the number of decimal digits in coordinate values MUST NOT be interpreted as an indication of accuracy. RSDGGS takes the opposite position: the number of bytes in the index IS the precision indicator, by design. This makes the RSDGGS encoding self-describing in a way that 'geo' URIs are not.

The 'geo' URI text encoding (typically 20-30 bytes for a full coordinate) is impractical for 802.15.4 MAC frames and CBOR-encoded IoT messages where wire efficiency is critical. The RSDGGS 1-8 byte binary encoding is 4-30 times more compact for equivalent precision.

RSDGGS MAY expose a 'geo' URI mapping for interoperability: an RSDGGS cell center can be expressed as a 'geo' URI with the u= parameter set to the cell radius. This mapping is lossy (the 'geo' URI does not encode the cell boundary shape) but suitable for human-readable display and web interoperability contexts. Implementations SHOULD provide this mapping for diagnostic and display purposes.

section.name: RFC 6442: Location Conveyance for SIP
section.t: RFC 6442 (Polk, Rosen, and Peterson, 2011) defines mechanisms for conveying geographic location information within the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). It is a Standards Track document. The primary use case is emergency services (E9-1-1, E1-1-2) and presence-based location sharing. It mandates use of the PIDF-LO (Presence Information Data Format — Location Object, RFC 4119) as the location representation format.

section.name: RFC 6442 Technical Approach
section.t: RFC 6442 introduces a Geolocation SIP header field that carries either a location-by-value (a PIDF-LO object embedded in the SIP message body) or a location-by-reference (a URI from which a PIDF-LO can be retrieved, typically via HTTP or SIP SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY). A new 424 (Bad Location Information) SIP response code is defined for cases where the location cannot be processed by the recipient.

PIDF-LO is an XML format carrying WGS-84 coordinates (point, circle, ellipse, polygon, or civic address). It includes uncertainty representation, confidence levels, and method-of-determination metadata (GPS, manual, cell-tower, etc.). SIP intermediaries are prohibited from modifying or deleting location data in transit. User consent is required before a UAC may include location in a SIP request.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 6442 / PIDF-LO RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Target protocol SIP (session signal.) 802.15.4 MAC, CBOR, IPv6 Location format PIDF-LO (~500 bytes) CBOR bstr (1-8 bytes) Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Device class SIP UA (smartphone) Constrained IoT (M) Routing use Geoloc-Routing hdr See Section 13 Privacy Consent/by-ref URI Trunc., RSL disclosure Uncertainty PIDF-LO conf/method Implicit in byte length Acquisition method GPS, cell-tower, manual Sec.11 coop. local.

section.t: RFC 6442's PIDF-LO XML representation is orders of magnitude larger than RSDGGS and requires XML parsing infrastructure wholly impractical on constrained IoT devices. The consent model defined in RFC 6442, requiring user authorization before location disclosure, addresses a real privacy concern. RSDGGS addresses the same concern through the truncation model: devices share only the resolution necessary for the purpose, with no infrastructure required to enforce the policy.

RFC 6442's Geolocation-Routing header enables SIP routing based on location. This is a routing hint at the application layer, not an address-arithmetic property of the network address itself. RSDGGS geographic IPv6 addressing (Section 13) achieves location-based routing at the network layer without any signaling overhead, as the routing metric is embedded in the destination address.

The two specifications are complementary: a SIP-capable IoT gateway MAY translate an RSDGGS cell to a PIDF-LO for interfaces toward SIP-based emergency services infrastructure, and vice versa. The translation is defined by the cell-center-to-lat/lon mapping with uncertainty equal to the cell radius.

section.name: RFC 9179: A YANG Grouping for Geographic Locations
section.t: RFC 9179 (Hopps, 2022) defines a reusable YANG grouping for geographic location data, intended for inclusion in YANG data models for network management. It is a Standards Track document. It is explicitly designed for YANG-managed network elements such as routers, switches, and base stations, not for constrained IoT endpoints.

section.name: RFC 9179 Technical Approach
section.t: The geo-location YANG grouping includes: a reference-frame specifying the astronomical body and geodetic datum (defaulting to WGS-84 Earth); a location choice between ellipsoidal coordinates (latitude as decimal64 with 16 fraction-digits, longitude as decimal64 with 16 fraction-digits, optional height in meters) or Cartesian coordinates (x, y, z in meters); a velocity vector (v-north, v-east, v-up in meters per second with 12 fraction-digits); and timestamp and valid-until fields. Coordinate accuracy is carried as a separate decimal64 field in meters.

The design is notable for its explicit support for non-Earth astronomical bodies (Mars, the Moon, etc.) through the reference-frame mechanism, and for velocity as a first-class field. It is intended as a reusable module embedded in other YANG models, not as a standalone protocol.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 9179 YANG grouping RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Target context YANG/NETCONF mgmt 802.15.4 / CBOR / IPv6 Encoding XML/JSON (NETCONF) CBOR bstr (1-8 bytes) Precision decimal64 (16 frac) 3 cm at 8 bytes Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Routing use Not defined See Section 13 Constrained devices Not applicable Primary target Uncertainty coord-accuracy (m) Implicit in byte length Velocity v-north, v-east, v-up EKF state (Sec.11)

section.t: RFC 9179's decimal64 latitude and longitude fields (16 fraction-digits) provide sub-nanometer theoretical precision, far exceeding GPS capability. RSDGGS at 8 bytes provides 3 cm precision, which matches or exceeds operational GPS accuracy for IoT applications. The YANG encoding overhead (XML or JSON field names plus decimal values) is typically 60-100 bytes per location fix versus 1-8 bytes for RSDGGS.

RFC 9179 does not define a hierarchical structure for location data and provides no support for location-based routing. The RSDGGS cell index has no analog in the RFC 9179 model. An RSDGGS extension to the RFC 9179 grouping is a potential future work item, adding an optional rsdggs-cell leaf of type binary with length constraint 1..8 to the geo-location grouping, enabling network elements to carry RSDGGS regulatory context alongside their WGS-84 coordinates in YANG data models.

section.name: RFC 9632: Finding and Using Geofeed Data
section.t: RFC 9632 (Bush, Candela, Kumari, and Housley, 2024) specifies how IP address holders publish authoritative geographic location data for their address space using geofeed CSV files, and how consumers discover and authenticate these files using RPSL inetnum objects and RPKI signatures. It obsoletes RFC 9092. The underlying geofeed format is defined in RFC 8805.

section.name: RFC 9632 Technical Approach
section.t: A geofeed file is a CSV document published at a stable HTTPS URL, containing rows of the form: IP-prefix, country-code, region-code, city-name, postal-code (deprecated). The file maps IP address prefixes to political-administrative geographic designators (ISO 3166-1 country codes, ISO 3166-2 region codes). Discovery is via a geofeed: attribute in the RPSL inetnum: object for the relevant address range. Authentication uses RPKI Resource Certificates with CMS signatures; a new EE certificate is generated for each file version.

Geofeed granularity is at the IP prefix level: a /24 prefix may be mapped to a city, a /16 to a country. The most specific inetnum: object with a geofeed reference governs, and geofeed data may have finer granularity than the inetnum: block itself. The format intentionally omits precise coordinate data: the mapping is to political-administrative units, not WGS-84 coordinates.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 9632 Geofeed RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Address space IP prefixes (BGP) 802.15.4 / 6LoWPAN / CBOR Loc. granularity Country/region/city 3cm-continental (8B) Format CSV file (HTTPS) Binary (1-8B in-frame) Discovery RPSL inetnum + RPKI MAC bcn/RSDGGS IPv6 Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Real-time use Batch/periodic fetch Per-frame/per-packet Device class BGP routers, servers Constrained IoT (M) Routing Not defined See Section 13

section.t: RFC 9632 and RSDGGS address fundamentally different layers of the same problem. RFC 9632 maps IP address blocks — which are administratively assigned and may not correspond to the physical location of the device using them — to geographic designators, for the purpose of correcting commercial geolocation database errors. RSDGGS encodes the physical location of an IoT device directly in a binary index that travels with every message the device sends, for the purpose of regulatory compliance determination at the MAC layer.

A meaningful integration point exists: RSDGGS-IPv6 geographic addresses (Section 13) are by definition location-accurate. An operator deploying RSDGGS-IPv6 addresses could publish a geofeed file trivially, as the address prefix directly encodes the geographic region. A /72 RSDGGS-IPv6 prefix geofeed entry maps to a single dodecahedron face (ITU Region); a /88 prefix maps to a country-scale cell. This makes RSDGGS-IPv6 deployments inherently geofeed-compliant without the mismatch that arises when administratively assigned IP prefixes are spread across multiple geographic regions.

section.name: RFC 8805: A Format for Self-Published IP Geolocation Feeds
section.t: RFC 8805 (Kline, Duleba, Szamonek, Moser, and Kumari, 2020) defines the geofeed CSV format that RFC 9632 subsequently standardized discovery for. It is an Independent Submission Informational RFC. The format was developed at Google to address cases where regional network operators needed to rapidly publish corrections to commercial geolocation database errors.

section.name: RFC 8805 Technical Approach
section.t: A geofeed file is a UTF-8 CSV text file published at a stable HTTPS URL. Each non-comment line has the form: ip_prefix, alpha2code, region, city, postal_code. The IP prefix field is required; all others are optional. The format intentionally only allows coarse-level location — political-administrative designators (ISO 3166-1 country code, ISO 3166-2 region code, city name) rather than precise coordinates. Postal code is included for backward compatibility but its use is deprecated. The file is self-published by the IP address holder and consumed by geolocation data pipeline operators on a polling schedule.

RFC 8805 is the predecessor to RFC 9632 and directly defines the data format that RFC 9632 provides discovery mechanisms for. The two documents form a coupled pair: RFC 8805 is the format specification; RFC 9632 is the discovery and authentication specification.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 8805 Geofeed Format RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Target IP prefix holders IoT device manufacturers Granularity Country/region/city 3cm-continental (8B) Format CSV text (HTTPS poll) Binary (1-8B in-frame) Update mechanism Periodic HTTP fetch Per-frame dynamic Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Constrained devices Not applicable Primary target Precision Administrative boundary Physical loc, metered

section.t: RFC 8805 and RSDGGS share the property of being self-published: an IP address holder publishes a geofeed file asserting the location of their prefix, and an IoT device encodes its RSDGGS cell asserting its own location. The trust models differ significantly: geofeed authenticity in RFC 8805 relies on RPKI (via RFC 9632) binding the file to the address holder's certificate; RSDGGS cell authenticity in peer-assisted scenarios relies on the MAC-layer STS authentication defined in Section 11.4.2 and the multi-peer confidence model of Section 10.3.

As noted in Section 15.5, RSDGGS-IPv6 geographic addresses (Section 13) are inherently geofeed-compatible: the address prefix encodes geographic location by definition, eliminating the mismatch between administratively assigned IP prefixes and their physical locations that RFC 8805 was designed to correct.

section.name: RFC 5808: Requirements for a Location-by-Reference Mechanism
section.t: RFC 5808 (Marshall, 2010) is an Informational document from the IETF GEOPRIV working group that defines requirements for Location-by-Reference (LbyR) mechanisms. It is part of the GEOPRIV architecture family that includes RFC 6280, RFC 5491, and RFC 6772. It explicitly leaves Location-by-Value (LbyV) out of scope.

section.name: RFC 5808 Technical Approach
section.t: RFC 5808 defines the LbyR lifecycle as comprising four stages: Location URI Creation (at a Location Information Server, LIS); Location URI Distribution (via a Location Configuration Protocol, LCP, from LIS to Target); Location URI Conveyance (from Target to Location Recipient via a signaling protocol such as SIP); and Location URI Dereferencing (Location Recipient resolves the URI to obtain a PIDF-LO). The dereference protocol must support URI-form location references, must authenticate both client and server, and must return a well-formed PIDF-LO document.

The motivation for LbyR is that in mobile networks it is not efficient for an end host to periodically query a LIS for up-to-date location. Instead, the LIS holds the current location and the Target carries only a URI reference, which can be dereferenced by authorized recipients to obtain the current location at the time of dereference.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 5808 LbyR Req. RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Architecture LIS + LCP + dereference Self-contained index Infrastructure req. Location Info. Server None (no server) Location currency Via dereference Carried in-frame, updated Constrained devices Not addressed Primary target Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Privacy model Rule Maker + LIS policy Structural (truncation) Location form PIDF-LO (after deref) CBOR bstr (direct)

section.t: The LbyR architecture requires persistent network connectivity to a Location Information Server for location dereferencing. This is fundamentally incompatible with the operational model of 802.15.4 IoT devices, which may operate in disconnected or intermittently connected environments, cannot carry TCP/TLS stacks required for HTTPS dereferencing, and must determine regulatory context before establishing any network connection at all.

RSDGGS takes the Location-by-Value position for IoT: the location index is carried directly in the MAC frame or IPv6 address. The RSDGGS cooperative localization mechanism (Section 11) is analogous to the LIS in the RFC 5808 architecture, but is fully distributed and requires no server infrastructure: the network of peers collectively provides the location determination function that RFC 5808 centralizes in a LIS.

section.name: RFC 5491: GEOPRIV PIDF-LO Usage Clarification, Considerations, and Recommendations
section.t: RFC 5491 (Winterbottom, Thomson, and Tschofenig, 2009) is a Standards Track document that clarifies usage rules for the PIDF-LO format originally defined in RFC 4119. It is part of the GEOPRIV family and serves as the normative usage guide for the location object format that underlies RFC 6442, RFC 5808, RFC 6280, and RFC 6772.

section.name: RFC 5491 Technical Approach
section.t: RFC 5491 defines seven rules for constructing PIDF-LO documents. The key rules relevant to RSDGGS comparison are: Rule 4 specifies that providing more than one location chunk in a single location-info element should be avoided; Rules 5 and 6 govern when compound location is permitted, requiring that multiple chunks come from the same source at the same time by the same determination method; Rule 7 requires that coarse location be provided before fine location in compound representations.

RFC 5491 defines two location representation types within PIDF-LO: geodetic location (WGS-84 coordinates, GML geometry shapes including Point, Circle, Ellipse, ArcBand, Polygon) and civic location (structured address: country, administrative regions A1-A6, street, floor, room). The GML subset defined for geodetic location requires mandatory implementation for location-based routing applications.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 5491 PIDF-LO Usage RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Location types Geodetic + civic (addr.) Geographic cell only Compound location Rules 4-7 (XML elems) Single hier. index Uncertainty GML shape (poly/circle) Implicit in byte length Coarse-to-fine Rule 7 (explicit) Structural (MSB→LSB) Encoding XML/GML (~2000 bytes) Binary (1-8 bytes) Floor / room Civic element supported Not defined Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Constrained devices Not addressed Primary target

section.t: RFC 5491's Rule 7 — coarse location MUST precede fine location in compound PIDF-LO — is structurally expressed in RSDGGS by the bit layout itself: Byte 0 (coarsest) precedes Byte 7 (finest), and truncation from the right always yields the coarser representation. RSDGGS embodies Rule 7 as an invariant property of the encoding rather than an application-layer behavioral requirement.

RFC 5491 supports civic location (floor number, room identifier) as a compound element alongside geodetic coordinates. RSDGGS does not encode civic location. For indoor deployments requiring floor-level regulatory distinction (which is uncommon for ISM band rules but relevant for UWB power limits in some jurisdictions), a civic layer MAY be carried as a separate CBOR field alongside the RSDGGS cell, using the PIDF-LO civic format or a simplified representation.

section.name: RFC 6280: An Architecture for Location and Location Privacy in Internet Applications
section.t: RFC 6280 (Barnes, Lepinski, Cooper, Morris, Tschofenig, and Schulzrinne, 2011) is a Best Current Practice document that describes the GEOPRIV architecture for privacy-preserving location-based services. It consolidates and expands on the original GEOPRIV requirements from RFC 3693 and serves as the architectural foundation for the entire GEOPRIV family of specifications.

section.name: RFC 6280 Technical Approach
section.t: The central component of the GEOPRIV architecture is the Location Object (LO), which binds location information to user-specified privacy rules. The architecture defines five roles: Location Generator (LG), which produces raw location measurements; Location Server (LS), which stores location objects and enforces privacy rules; Rule Maker (RM), which is the user or device owner who specifies privacy preferences; Target, the entity whose location is being described; and Location Recipient (LR), which consumes location information.

A central feature of the GEOPRIV architecture is that location information is always bound to privacy rules. These rules govern who may receive the location, how precisely, and under what conditions. The privacy protections rely on recipients honoring the rules they receive alongside the location data; RFC 6280 acknowledges that technical enforcement is inherently limited and relies on legal and contractual mechanisms for compliance assurance.

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 6280 GEOPRIV Arch. RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Privacy model Rule-based (RM+LS+LR) Struct. byte trunc. Infrastructure LG + LS + LR servers None required Enforcement Honor-system + legal No over-disclosure Location binding LO + privacy rules obj. Single CBOR byte string Constrained devices Not addressed Primary target Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Rule distribution XCAP/presence protocol Not applicable Trust model Centralized (LS) Distributed (peer mesh)

section.t: The GEOPRIV architecture's privacy model requires that the Rule Maker express privacy preferences, that the Location Server enforce them, and that Location Recipients honor them. This three-party trust model requires persistent infrastructure that is unavailable to constrained IoT devices operating in disconnected environments.

RSDGGS replaces the GEOPRIV rule-based privacy model with structural privacy: a device that shares a 3-byte RSDGGS cell is physically incapable of disclosing more than country-level location, regardless of recipient behavior. No rules, servers, or trust relationships are required to enforce this property. The privacy level is determined by the sender's choice of index length, not by the recipient's compliance with transmitted rules.

This structural approach is both stronger (cannot be violated by a non-compliant recipient) and weaker (cannot express nuanced rules like 'share with spouse but not employer') than the GEOPRIV model. For ISM regulatory compliance, where the only required disclosure is 'am I in ITU Region 2?', the structural model is entirely sufficient. RSDGGS implementations that require nuanced privacy rules for non-regulatory purposes MAY layer a RFC 6772 geolocation policy document alongside the RSDGGS cell in application-layer CBOR messages.

section.name: RFC 6772: Geolocation Policy: A Document Format for Expressing Privacy Preferences for Location Information
section.t: RFC 6772 (Schulzrinne, Tschofenig, Cuellar, Polk, Morris, and Thomson, 2013) is a Standards Track document that defines an XML document format for expressing location privacy preferences within the GEOPRIV architecture. It extends the Common Policy schema (RFC 4745) with location-specific conditions and transformations.

section.name: RFC 6772 Technical Approach
section.t: A geolocation authorization document is an XML document with MIME type application/auth-policy+xml, using the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:geolocation-policy. Documents are structured as sets of rules, each containing a condition, an action, and a transformation component. Conditions may include identity-based conditions (who is requesting) and location-based conditions (where the target is). Transformations specify how the location information should be modified before delivery — for example, reducing precision by replacing a precise geodetic coordinate with a less precise one, or replacing geodetic coordinates with a civic address.

Documents are stored and managed using XCAP (XML Configuration Access Protocol, RFC 4825) at a Location Server or Presence Server. The Rule Maker uses XCAP to create, modify, and delete authorization policies. Location-based conditions allow policies such as 'when I am at work, share my location with my employer at city-level precision; when I am at home, share with family at room-level precision.'

section.name: Gaps Addressed by RSDGGS

figure.artwork: Dimension RFC 6772 Geoloc. Policy RSDGGS ─────────────────── ──────────────────────── ───────────────────────── Privacy mechanism XML policy rules + XCAP Struct. byte trunc. Infrastructure XCAP server + LS req. None Loc. obfuscation Precision reduction Byte trunc. (binary) Enforcement Recipient compliance Structural impossib. Constrained devices Not addressed Primary target Encoding XML (hundreds of bytes) N/A (no policy doc) Regulatory context Absent Primary design goal Policy expressive. High (identity+loc.) Single dim (resolution)

section.t: RFC 6772's location obfuscation mechanism — reducing precision in the transformation element of a policy rule — is conceptually identical to RSDGGS truncation, but implemented through a server-side XML transformation rather than a structural property of the encoding. The RFC 6772 approach requires a Location Server to apply the transformation rule; the RSDGGS approach requires the transmitting device to select an index length. The RSDGGS approach is implementable on a 32-byte RAM microcontroller with no server dependency.

RFC 6772's location-based conditions — rules that apply differently depending on where the Target is — have a direct analogy in RSDGGS: the RSL (Resolution Sufficiency Level) table defines location-dependent disclosure requirements for regulatory purposes. A device in Face 2 (North America) needs to disclose only 1 byte to establish 902 MHz legality; a device in Face 3 (East Asia) needs 3 bytes to distinguish Japan from China. The RSDGGS RSL table is a regulatory-specific, infrastructure-free analog to RFC 6772's location-based policy conditions.

The two mechanisms are composable for deployments requiring both regulatory compliance and user privacy management: RSDGGS provides the minimum regulatory disclosure at the MAC layer; a separate RFC 6772 geolocation policy governs higher-precision disclosure for application-layer services requiring richer location context.

section.name: Backward Citations: Relevant References Within Cited Documents
section.t: Each patent and RFC examined in Section 16 carries its own citation list. This section identifies references within those backward citation chains that are independently relevant to RSDGGS — documents cited by the cited documents that surface additional prior art, gaps, or informative context not already addressed in the specification.

section.name: GPSR — Greedy Perimeter Stateless Routing (from US 10,812,365)
section.t: Karp, B. and H.T. Kung, 'GPSR: Greedy Perimeter Stateless Routing for Wireless Networks', MobiCom 2000. Cited as primary prior art in US 10,812,365 (geohyperbolic routing patent).

Relevance to RSDGGS: GPSR is the canonical geographic greedy forwarding algorithm for wireless networks. It defines two components: greedy forwarding (advance toward destination by geographic distance) and perimeter routing (traverse face of a planar graph when greedy forwarding is stuck at a void). RSDGGS Section 15.3 defines geographic greedy forwarding using common-prefix-length as the proximity metric but does not define a void-handling mechanism. GPSR's perimeter routing is a direct gap in RSDGGS. Implementations in sparse networks where geographic voids may exist SHOULD implement a fallback void handler; GPSR's perimeter routing or AODV-RPL (RFC 9854) route discovery are the recommended candidates. This gap should be documented as a known limitation in Section 15.3.

section.name: IEEE 802.11d — Country Information Elements (from US 10,306,400 family)
section.t: IEEE 802.11d-2001, 'Amendment: Specifications for Operation in Additional Regulatory Domains'. Surfaced through the wireless regulatory compliance patent family (US 10,306,400, US 9,654,965).

Relevance to RSDGGS: IEEE 802.11d defines country information elements (Country IE) in Wi-Fi beacon frames. Each Country IE contains a 3-character country string and per-channel maximum transmit power tables. This is the direct 802.11 predecessor of the RSDGGS 802.15.4 Location Sub-IE defined in Section 14. The comparison is instructive: 802.11d uses a flat country string as the regulatory identifier, limiting it to coarse national granularity with no hierarchy, no privacy truncation, and no regulatory parameter encoding beyond max power per channel. RSDGGS replaces the flat country string with a hierarchical cell index that encodes ITU Region at 1 byte, country-scale at 3 bytes, and sub-national detail at 4-6 bytes, while the regulatory database carries the full parameter set. The RSDGGS Sub-IE should be cited as a hierarchical extension of the 802.11d Country IE concept to 802.15.4 with ITU-regional alignment.

section.name: IEEE 802.11h — DFS and TPC (from US 10,306,400 family)
section.t: IEEE 802.11h-2003, 'Spectrum and Transmit Power Management Extensions'. Also surfaced through the wireless regulatory compliance patent family.

Relevance to RSDGGS: IEEE 802.11h defines Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) for radar avoidance and Transmit Power Control (TPC) for regulatory compliance in the 5 GHz band. TPC specifically defines a negotiated reduction of transmit power between stations based on measured path loss, with the goal of keeping transmit power at the minimum needed for link quality. This is the direct 802.11 predecessor of RSDGGS Section 10.4 (adaptive power control at regulatory boundaries). The key difference: 802.11h TPC is link-quality-driven and reactive, reducing power when the link permits. RSDGGS boundary power control is geography-driven and proactive, reducing power as a device approaches a regulatory boundary regardless of link quality. The two mechanisms are complementary and both should apply in deployments near regulatory boundaries.

section.name: RFC 3693 — GEOPRIV Requirements (from RFC 6442 and RFC 6280)
section.t: Cuellar, J., Morris, J., Mulligan, D., Peterson, J., and J. Polk, 'Geopriv Requirements', RFC 3693, February 2004. Cited as the foundational requirements document by both RFC 6442 and RFC 6280.

Relevance to RSDGGS: RFC 3693 defines the concept of a 'using protocol': any protocol that transmits or acts on location information must satisfy GEOPRIV's authorization, integrity, and privacy requirements. RSDGGS's 802.15.4 MAC bootstrap (Section 14) qualifies as a using protocol under RFC 3693's definition: it transmits location information (the RSDGGS cell) in MAC frames and acts on it to configure regulatory parameters. RSDGGS satisfies RFC 3693's privacy requirement through structural truncation (G3, G8) rather than policy rules, satisfies the integrity requirement through STS-authenticated ranging (Section 13.4.2) rather than digital signatures, and satisfies the authorization requirement through the MAC association process (only devices that have joined the PAN receive beacon location information). RFC 3693 should be cited as an informative reference in Section 14.

section.name: RFC 3825 — DHCP Geodetic Location Option (from RFC 5870 and RFC 5808)
section.t: Polk, J., Schnizlein, J., and M. Linsner, 'Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol Option for Coordinate-based Location Configuration Information', RFC 3825, July 2004. Cited as a location provisioning mechanism in RFC 5870 and RFC 5808.

Relevance and limitation: RFC 3825 defines a DHCP option carrying WGS-84 latitude and longitude for device location provisioning. A DHCPv6 analog carrying an RSDGGS cell index would provide a convenient provisioning path for fixed-infrastructure deployments where DHCP already runs. However, RFC 3825 and any DHCPv6 RSDGGS extension are explicitly excluded from serving as a required provisioning mechanism by design goal G8.

The reason is structural: DHCP is a client-server protocol with a centralized server as a single point of failure. If the DHCPv6 server is unavailable — due to server failure, network partition, or initial bootstrap before any infrastructure is established — onboarding devices cannot acquire their regulatory configuration. This violates G8's requirement for complete independence from any centralized server. IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC, RFC 4862) and Neighbor Discovery (RFC 4861) demonstrate the correct architectural model: a device derives its IPv6 address from its MAC address and the subnet prefix advertised by neighboring routers, with no server dependency. RSDGGS follows the same model: a device derives its regulatory cell from the RSDGGS cells of neighboring devices (Section 11), with no server dependency.

RFC 3825 / DHCPv6 RSDGGS options MAY be implemented as optional accelerators in managed infrastructure deployments where the DHCP server is always available before devices are deployed. They MUST NOT be implemented as the sole or primary regulatory provisioning path. Any RSDGGS implementation that supports DHCPv6 provisioning MUST also implement the peer-assisted bootstrap of Section 11 as a fallback, and MUST fall back to peer-assisted bootstrap automatically if the DHCP server does not respond within a configurable timeout.

section.name: RFC 4632 — CIDR: Classless Inter-Domain Routing (from RFC 9632)
section.t: Fuller, V. and T. Li, 'Classless Inter-domain Routing (CIDR): The Internet Address Assignment and Aggregation Plan', BCP 122, RFC 4632, August 2006. Cited as background in RFC 9632's geofeed discovery context.

Relevance to RSDGGS: CIDR defines prefix-based aggregation of IPv4 address space into routing hierarchies, where a /16 prefix aggregates 65,536 /32 host addresses into a single routing entry. RSDGGS-IPv6 geographic addressing (Section 15) implements the same concept with geographic cells: a /72 RSDGGS-IPv6 prefix aggregates all devices in a single dodecahedron face (ITU Region) into a single routing entry; a /88 prefix aggregates all devices in a country-scale cell. The mathematical relationship is direct — RSDGGS-IPv6 is CIDR for geography rather than administrative address allocation. RFC 4632 should be cited as an informative reference in Section 15.2 to establish this conceptual lineage.

section.name: RFC 6269 — Issues with IP Address Sharing (from RFC 9632)
section.t: Ford, M., Boucadair, M., Durand, A., Levis, P., and P. Roberts, 'Issues with IP Address Sharing', RFC 6269, June 2011. Cited in RFC 9632's introduction as motivation for geofeed.

Relevance to RSDGGS: RFC 6269 documents the problem that commercial IP geolocation databases are unreliable when IP addresses are shared (NAT, CGN, mobile carrier address pools) because a shared address maps to many physical locations. RFC 9632 geofeed was designed as a partial solution — operators can publish authoritative location for their IP prefix. RSDGGS-IPv6 geographic addressing solves this problem categorically for devices using RSDGGS addresses: the lower 64 bits of the IPv6 address encode the device's geographic cell, making location-by-address exact by construction rather than inferred. This should be noted in Section 15 as one of the concrete advantages of RSDGGS-IPv6 over commercial geolocation.

section.name: GeoCast — Geographic Addressing and Routing (from RFC 2009)
section.t: Navas, J.C. and T. Imielinski, 'GeoCast: Geographic Addressing and Routing', MobiCom 1997. Cited in RFC 2009 as the companion paper describing geographic multicast.

Relevance to RSDGGS: GeoCast defines geographic multicast: delivering a packet to all nodes currently within a specified geographic polygon. RSDGGS-IPv6 prefix aggregation enables a direct implementation of GeoCast: a packet addressed to a /72 RSDGGS-IPv6 prefix is a GeoCast to all devices in a single ITU Region; a packet addressed to a /88 prefix is a GeoCast to a country-scale cell. This is lossless GeoCast — the cell boundary is exact, not approximated by a polygon. GeoCast should be cited as an informative reference in Section 15 as an ancestor of RSDGGS geographic multicast capability.

section.name: Summary of Newly Identified References
section.t: The following references, surfaced from the backward citation chains of documents already examined, should be added to Section 21 (References) of this draft as informative references:

Of these, RFC 3825 with its DHCP single-point-of-failure limitation, IEEE 802.11d as the direct predecessor of the RSDGGS 802.15.4 Sub-IE, and RFC 4862/4861 as the SLAAC/ND model that G8 follows are the highest-priority additions. The GPSR void-handling gap is the most significant technical limitation currently undocumented in the specification.

section.name: Freedom to Operate and Prior Art Considerations
section.t: This section provides a comprehensive analysis of all patents and RFC standards examined during the development of RSDGGS. For each, it identifies the technical relationship to RSDGGS, evaluates freedom to operate, and identifies any improvement opportunity that the prior work suggests for RSDGGS. Improvement opportunities are RSDGGS-applicable enhancements that are either enabled by, or would have been blocked by, the referenced work. All patent analyses are informational only and do not constitute legal advice.

section.name: Expired Patents — Public Domain Prior Art
section.t: The following patents are expired and their full technical disclosures are in the public domain. They constitute prior art against any third-party attempt to patent the techniques they disclose, and RSDGGS implementations may freely use these techniques without license.

section.name: US Patent 4,939,726 — Metricom, Inc. (Expired 2007)
section.t: Title: Method for Routing Packets in a Packet Communication Network. Inventors: Flammer, Kalkwarf. Assignee: Metricom, Inc. (later Proxim Wireless Corp.). Filed 1989, granted July 3, 1990, expired 2007. Companion patent US 5,115,433 (Baran, Flammer, Kalkwarf — Metricom, 1992) is also expired.

figure.artwork:
Key claims (now public domain): Claim 1: Node identifier indicative of geographic location referenced to a terrestrial coordinate grid Claim 1: Routing by maximum forward geographic progress without routing directory or table Claim 3: Lock table with neighbor link quality factor based on distance, power, retry, throughput, delay Claim 5: Weighted link quality factor for preferred paths
US 5,115,433 adds (also public domain): Selection of forwarding node by minimum power required Link quality criteria include: net data rate, network delay, data priority — richer than Claim 3 of 4,939,726

section.t: RSDGGS improvement opportunity — Link Quality Weighted Forwarding: US 4,939,726 Claim 3 and US 5,115,433 define a link quality (LQ) factor incorporating distance, power, retry history, throughput, and delay. RSDGGS Section 15.3 defines geographic greedy forwarding using only common-prefix-length as the progress metric. Incorporating a link quality weighting that prefers the LQ-best neighbor among those making geographic progress would improve real-world routing performance in dense ISM-band deployments where RSSI and retry rates vary significantly. This enhancement is freely implementable from the expired public domain claims and should be noted as a normative extension candidate for follow-on standards-track work.

section.name: US Patent 6,982,966 — Status Unconfirmed
section.t: This number was not definitively identified in patent database searches. If this patent was cited in relation to geographic routing or MANET protocols, the Metricom prior art (4,939,726 and 5,115,433, both expired 2007 and 2009 respectively) predates any 2006-era geographic routing patent by 15+ years and establishes the core concepts as public domain. Independent verification at patents.uspto.gov is still recommended.

section.name: US Patent 10,306,400 / Application 2014/0162692 — Wirelesss Regulatory Compliance (Active until ~2035)
section.t: Title: Systems and Methods for Enforcing Wireless Regulatory Compliance. Assignee not publicly confirmed from application number alone; the issued patent US 10,306,400 covers a thermostat and home network device context. Filed as US Application 20140162692 approximately 2013-2014. The issued patent family includes related grants US 9,794,738 and US 9,654,965. Active.

figure.artwork:
Core claim element (all related patents): Determining geographic location of a device Configuring device to operate on a channel set based on location VERIFYING location by analyzing AC power line frequency (50 Hz = European / Region 1; 60 Hz = American / Region 2) Re-configuring if verification fails Claim 7: Explicitly covers devices devoid of cellular and GPS
US 9,654,965 adds: Lookup table / database mapping location to regulations Table may be stored locally or downloaded from network Location determined from GNSS, MCC, AP country codes, indirect AP location, or cell tower information

section.t: RSDGGS freedom to operate: RSDGGS does not use power line frequency as a location verification mechanism. The core novelty of this patent family is the AC frequency verification step, which is absent from RSDGGS entirely. RSDGGS derives location from: pre-provisioned cell index (Section 12), peer-received RSDGGS beacons (Section 11), or cooperative ranging (Section 13). None of these mechanisms involve power line analysis. No claim element reads on RSDGGS.

RSDGGS improvement opportunity — Lookup Table Architecture: US 9,654,965 explicitly discloses the architecture of a location-to-regulations lookup table stored locally on the device, optionally small enough to fit in embedded memory, potentially updated from network. This is directly analogous to the RSDGGS regulatory database architecture defined in Section 8. The patent discloses this as a WLAN channel compliance mechanism; RSDGGS generalizes it to ISM bands with a hierarchical geographic index as the lookup key. Because 9,654,965 is active, RSDGGS implementations MUST NOT incorporate AC power line frequency as a location verification step alongside the lookup table. The lookup table architecture itself predates 9,654,965 as prior art (RFC 2009 describes location-to-routing-table mapping from 1996), but the specific combination of local storage + network update + GNSS/MCC/AP location sources for the lookup key is a design pattern that RSDGGS implementations should credit to this work in any patent prosecution.

section.name: US Patent 10,812,365 — Geohyperbolic Routing (Northeastern University, Active until 2037)
section.t: Title: Geohyperbolic Routing and Addressing Schemes for Networks. Inventors: Dmitri Krioukov, Ivan Voitalov. Assignee: Northeastern University, Boston. Filed November 16, 2017. Granted October 20, 2020. Active, expires December 25, 2037.

figure.artwork:
Core claim elements: Network address = (r_i, theta_i, phi_i) in 3D hyperbolic space theta_i, phi_i = lat/lon mapped to angular coordinates r_i = centrality derived from population density zone rank Routing = greedy forwarding minimizing HYPERBOLIC DISTANCE Topology construction = connect to m geographically nearest neighbors; network reproduces Internet power-law topology CPC H04L2101/69: geographic information in network address CPC H04W40/20: route selection based on geographic position
RSDGGS distinguishing elements (no infringement): No hyperbolic space — RSDGGS uses integer cell index No radial centrality component — no population density Forwarding metric = common-prefix-length (XOR+CLZ), not hyperbolic distance Topology independent of population density zone ranking Face assignment = ITU regulatory zones, not Internet-scale power-law topology reproduction

section.t: RSDGGS improvement opportunity — None applicable: The geohyperbolic model is specifically optimized for large-scale Internet backbone topology reproduction, using population-density centrality to reproduce power-law degree distributions. RSDGGS targets constrained 802.15.4 IoT mesh networks with no backbone topology requirements and no population-density data available at compile time on embedded devices. The mathematical approaches are incompatible at a fundamental level: hyperbolic geometry requires floating-point (r, theta, phi) arithmetic, whereas RSDGGS's design goal G4 requires no-FPU integer arithmetic. No improvement opportunity from this patent is applicable to RSDGGS.

Backward citations of interest: US 10,812,365 cites US 8,284,788 (Krioukov et al., hyperbolic network embedding, 2012) as a predecessor. The academic paper by Krioukov et al. 'Hyperbolic Geometry of Complex Networks' (Physical Review E, 2010) is the underlying research. Both establish that hyperbolic geometry for Internet-scale routing is a well-developed research area distinct from RSDGGS's approach.

section.name: US Patent 11,652,742 — Ghost Routing (Microsoft, Active until 2041)

section.name: CN101923801B — Method for Generating a Regular Dodecahedron Map Projection (Expired)
section.t: Assignee: Wuhan University (WHU), Wuhan, China. Inventors: Hu Peng, Li Yunxiang, Zhu Fuli. Application number: CN2009100626550A. Filing and priority date: 10 June 2009. Grant date: 29 February 2012. Jurisdiction: China only (no PCT application, no US, EP, or other national-phase equivalents identified). Legal status: Expired — Fee Related. Anticipated statutory expiration: 10 June 2029 (20-year term from filing). Actual status: lapsed prior to statutory expiration due to non-payment of annual maintenance fees.

Legal status note: 'Expired — Fee Related' = patent lapsed due to non-payment of annual maintenance fees under Chinese patent law. The claims entered the public domain at the date of lapse. The 2029 anticipated expiration date is the statutory maximum; the actual lapse occurred earlier. The patent is unenforceable and cannot be asserted against any implementer anywhere.
Jurisdiction note: CN101923801B is a Chinese national patent only. No PCT (international) application was filed. No US, EP, JP, KR, or other national-phase equivalents exist. Even if the patent were active, its territorial scope would be limited to China and could not be enforced in the United States, European Union, or other IETF-relevant jurisdictions.

section.t: The method disclosed in CN101923801B describes a cartographic rendering pipeline for producing physical dodecahedron map products. The claimed method orients the dodecahedron so that one vertex coincides with the Earth's geographic North Pole and the antipodal vertex with the South Pole, selects a user-defined region of interest to determine each face's central meridian, applies a gnomonic projection per face to transform geographic vector data, clips the result to each pentagonal boundary, and outputs twelve pentagonal paper maps for assembly into a physical dodecahedron. The implementation is explicitly tied to ArcGIS and ESRI Shapefile data formats as the required geographic data pipeline.

Output artifact: visual cartographic map product (paper maps) Data pipeline: ArcGIS / ArcMap / ESRI Shapefile (.lyr, .shp) Purpose: Geographic visualization and education
RSDGGS distinguishing elements — no claim reads on RSDGGS: D1: Orientation — RSDGGS orients Face 2 at 39°N, 98°W (ITU Region 2 anchor); not North/South Pole alignment D2: Face assignment — RSDGGS faces are fixed to ITU Radio Regions; no user-selected region of interest or central meridian determination step exists in RSDGGS D3: Output — RSDGGS produces a 1-8 byte integer cell index; it produces no map, no Shapefile, no visual output D4: Pipeline — RSDGGS uses no ArcGIS, ArcMap, or ESRI Shapefile; encoding is pure arithmetic on a unit sphere D5: Purpose — RSDGGS encodes regulatory jurisdiction for IoT ISM band compliance; CN101923801B renders maps D6: Physical artifact — RSDGGS specifies no physical object; CN101923801B explicitly claims a paper map assembly step

section.t: Freedom to operate conclusion: CN101923801B presents no freedom-to-operate concern for RSDGGS on three independent grounds, each sufficient alone. First, the patent is expired due to fee non-payment and its claims are in the public domain — no enforcement is possible regardless of claim scope. Second, the patent is China-jurisdiction only with no international equivalents, so even if active it could not be enforced in the United States, European Union, Japan, or any other IETF-process jurisdiction. Third, no claim element of CN101923801B reads on RSDGGS: the patent covers a cartographic rendering pipeline for producing visual map products from geographic vector data using ArcGIS tooling, whereas RSDGGS is a binary integer encoding scheme for IoT device regulatory context with no map output, no GIS pipeline, and no physical artifact. The shared concept of using a dodecahedron as an Earth reference surface is established prior art predating CN101923801B by decades, with the gnomonic polyhedral map projection appearing in academic cartography literature since at least the 1940s (Fuller, 1944, US Patent 2,393,676, expired 1963) and in peer-reviewed cartographic literature through the 1990s.

Prior art note: CN101923801B itself acknowledges that dodecahedron map projection is a known concept by framing its contribution as 'breaking through the limitation that the previous projection surface is a plane and a developable surface.' The gnomonic projection of the Earth onto a regular dodecahedron is explicitly not novel to CN101923801B — the claimed novelty is the specific ArcGIS-based rendering workflow and the face-by-face data extraction pipeline. RSDGGS's use of the dodecahedron as a hierarchical geographic index is therefore independently supported by prior art that predates CN101923801B, in addition to the non-infringement analysis above.

section.name: RFC Citation Improvement Opportunities
section.t: The following analysis reviews each RFC cited in Section 16 (Relationship to Prior Geographic Addressing Work) and Section 21 (References) for improvement opportunities: technical details in those RFCs that RSDGGS could incorporate, extend, or more precisely differentiate from.

section.name: RFC 2009 — GPS-Based Addressing (1996, Experimental/Legacy)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — Weak beacon concept: RFC 2009 Section 5.2 defines 'weak radio beacons' that broadcast a GPS address enabling indoor devices without GPS to adopt the beacon's address. This is structurally identical to RSDGGS Section 11's peer-assisted location discovery, but RFC 2009's approach is address adoption (the Naive Device copies the beacon's address) rather than address derivation (RSDGGS derives its own cell from the beacon's cell via intersection and ranging). RSDGGS should explicitly note this distinction: RFC 2009's approach loses geographic uniqueness for devices sharing an adopted address, whereas RSDGGS's intersection-and-ranging approach preserves geographic uniqueness. This distinction strengthens the novelty claim of Section 11.

Improvement opportunity — IGPSMP protocol gap: RFC 2009 proposes IGPSMP (Internet GPS Management Protocol) for router-to-router geographic service area exchange, with a polygon boundary representation. RSDGGS explicitly avoids polygon boundaries in favor of cell prefix hierarchy. Noting that RSDGGS's approach eliminates IGPSMP entirely (routing decisions from address arithmetic, no management protocol needed) more precisely characterizes RSDGGS's architectural simplification relative to RFC 2009.

section.name: RFC 5870 — geo URI Scheme (2010, Standards Track)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — Uncertainty parameter alignment: RFC 5870 Section 3.4 defines the u= parameter as the uncertainty radius in meters, explicitly stating that it represents the uncertainty of the location rather than a desired precision. RSDGGS's truncation model produces cells with a defined radius (cell diameter / 2), which is conceptually equivalent to u= but is structural rather than declared. The RSDGGS-to-geo-URI translation proposed in Section 16.2 should map cell radius to u=, but must note that RFC 5870 explicitly states u= MUST NOT be interpreted as a request for a certain level of precision from a location server. The cell radius is a guaranteed precision bound, not a request — a stronger property than RFC 5870's u= semantics.

Improvement opportunity — CRS extensibility: RFC 5870 Section 3.5 defines a crs= parameter for alternative coordinate reference systems (default WGS-84). A future RSDGGS-aware geo URI extension could define crs=rsdggs as a CRS identifier, with the URI carrying the RSDGGS cell hex string as the coordinate value. This would enable geo URI interoperability for RSDGGS cell references in web and messaging contexts without loss of the RSDGGS hierarchical structure. This is a concrete future work item for Section 21 of the draft.

section.name: RFC 6442 — Location Conveyance for SIP (2011, Standards Track)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — 424 error code applicability: RFC 6442 Section 6 defines the 424 (Bad Location Information) SIP response code for cases where location cannot be processed. For RSDGGS-SIP integration (a gateway translating RSDGGS cells to PIDF-LO for emergency services), this error code should be returned when the RSDGGS cell's resolution is insufficient for the requested service (e.g., a 1-byte cell when the SIP application requires country-level precision). Defining an RSDGGS-specific error sub-code for 'insufficient cell resolution' would improve SIP gateway interoperability.

Improvement opportunity — Geolocation-Routing header: RFC 6442 Section 8 defines a Geolocation-Routing SIP header that can be set to 'yes' to indicate that the location should influence routing. RSDGGS geographic IPv6 addresses (Section 15) embed routing information in the address itself, making the Geolocation-Routing header redundant for RSDGGS-addressed traffic. Explicitly noting this in the draft strengthens the architectural case for RSDGGS-IPv6 as a simplification over SIP-based geographic routing.

section.name: RFC 9179 — YANG Grouping for Geographic Locations (2022, Standards Track)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — Velocity field: RFC 9179 Section 5 defines velocity as a first-class field in the geo-location grouping: v-north, v-east, and v-up in meters/second with 12 fraction-digits precision. RSDGGS Section 13.7 (Extended Kalman Filter) defines a velocity component in the EKF state vector as cells-per-second, but the CDDL schema in Section 7.3 does not expose velocity externally. Adding an optional velocity field to the RSDGGS CBOR encoding — expressed in EKF cell units for constrained devices or as an RFC 9179-compatible (v-north, v-east) pair for gateway contexts — would improve interoperability with YANG-managed network infrastructure.

Improvement opportunity — Altitude encoding: RFC 9179 defines height above WGS-84 ellipsoid in meters as a decimal64 field. RSDGGS Section 7.3 includes an optional alt-m float16 field in the location CDDL. Float16 provides only ~3 significant decimal digits of altitude precision (~1 meter at low altitude, degrading above 1 km). For applications requiring RFC 9179-compatible altitude precision, the CDDL should provide an alternative float32 or decimal encoding. This is a minor schema enhancement that should be noted as a future revision item.

section.name: RFC 9632 / RFC 8805 — Geofeed Data (2024 / 2020)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — RSDGGS-IPv6 geofeed compliance: RFC 8805 Section 2.1 defines the geofeed CSV format with fields: ip_prefix, alpha2code, region, city, postal_code. RFC 9632 Section 4 defines how geofeed files are discovered via RPSL inetnum objects. RSDGGS-IPv6 addresses are inherently geofeed-compatible, as noted in Section 15, but the specific mapping has not been formalized. A concrete improvement: define a RSDGGS-IPv6 geofeed profile where ip_prefix encodes the RSDGGS face (/72) or country-scale cell (/88), alpha2code is derived from the face's ITU Region, and region is the face name from the RSDGGS face table. This profile would make RSDGGS-IPv6 deployments automatically RFC 9632-compliant without any additional geofeed file maintenance.

section.name: RFC 5808 — Location-by-Reference Requirements (2010, Informational)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — Dereference latency requirement: RFC 5808 Section 4.3 requires that a location URI dereference return the current location at the time of dereference, not the location at the time the URI was created. This requirement is irrelevant to RSDGGS LbyV (Location-by-Value) encoding, but it highlights a gap: RSDGGS does not define a staleness indicator for the cell index. A device that provisioned its cell at manufacturing time (Section 12) and has never moved still carries a potentially stale index. Adding an optional timestamp or age field to the CBOR encoding would allow receivers to determine whether the cell index is current-position or provisioned-position, analogous to RFC 5808's dereference-time semantics. This is a concrete CDDL enhancement for the next draft revision.

section.name: RFC 5491 — PIDF-LO Usage (2009, Standards Track)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — Confidence level encoding: RFC 5491 Section 5.5 defines a confidence attribute in PIDF-LO location shapes, expressing the probability (as a percentage) that the described region contains the true location. RSDGGS implicitly expresses 100% confidence that the true location is within the stated cell (by construction of the encoding: the cell is computed from the true coordinate, so it always contains that coordinate). However, for RSDGGS cells derived from peer-assisted localization (Section 13) where the cell is inferred rather than computed, the confidence may be lower. Adding an optional confidence field (uint8, percentage) to the CBOR location encoding would align RSDGGS with RFC 5491's confidence model and would be particularly useful for cells derived from the cell intersection method of Section 13.2.

section.name: RFC 6280 — GEOPRIV Architecture (2011, BCP)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — Rule Maker analog: RFC 6280 Section 5 defines the Rule Maker role: the entity (typically the device owner) who specifies what location information may be disclosed to whom. RSDGGS's structural privacy model (byte truncation) does not support rule-based disclosure. For deployments where different recipients should receive different resolution (e.g., a regulatory compliance server receives 3 bytes, a fleet tracking application receives 7 bytes), an application-layer resolution selection mechanism is needed. Defining a CBOR map structure that carries multiple truncated cells at different resolutions, labeled by intended recipient type, would provide a RSDGGS-native analog to RFC 6280's Rule Maker mechanism without requiring XCAP or a Location Server.

section.name: RFC 6772 — Geolocation Policy (2013, Standards Track)
section.t: Improvement opportunity — Location-based condition analog: RFC 6772 Section 8 defines location-based conditions in policy rules: rules that apply only when the Target is within a specified geographic region. RSDGGS's RSL (Resolution Sufficiency Level) table in Section 8.2 is a regulatory-driven analog to RFC 6772's location-based conditions, but applies uniformly without per-device policy variation. For deployments with site-specific privacy requirements (e.g., a factory that requires higher location precision within its boundary but coarser precision outside), an RSDGGS extension could define per-cell RSL overrides stored in the regulatory database exception table (Section 8.3). This would be the RSDGGS-native equivalent of RFC 6772's location-based policy conditions without XML or XCAP infrastructure.

section.t: The following table consolidates all actionable improvement opportunities identified from the cited patents and RFCs, categorized by implementation priority.

The highest-priority improvements — link quality weighted forwarding, RSDGGS-IPv6 geofeed profile, and the staleness field — represent concrete enhancements to the core specification that should be incorporated in the -01 revision. The medium-priority items are suitable for informational notes or future work statements in the current -00 draft. The low-priority items are candidates for companion specifications or implementation guidance documents.

section.name: Reference Implementation (Rust Pseudocode)
section.t: This section provides a complete reference implementation of the RSDGGS encoder in Rust pseudocode. The implementation is structured as a no_std, no_alloc crate suitable for deployment on constrained 802.15.4 devices. All algorithms are expressed in terms that map directly to the mathematical definitions in the preceding sections. Floating-point arithmetic (f64) is used for the encode path; a fixed-point variant suitable for devices without FPU is noted where applicable.

This is pseudocode intended to specify behavior precisely. A production implementation would require additional error handling, const evaluation of intermediate values, and platform-specific optimizations. The worked example at Section 20.10 provides a concrete verification vector.

section.name: Compile-Time Constants
section.t: All twelve face center unit vectors are precomputed constants derived from the dodecahedron orientation procedure defined in Section 4.3. Face 2 (RSDGGS index 0x02) is centered at (31.43N, 102.48W), with icosahedron vertex 8 (its dual vertex) placed at the regulatory anchor (39N, 98W). These constants are reproduced here at full f64 precision and MUST be used by all conforming implementations. The rotation algorithm from Section 4.3 is not invoked at runtime.

section.name: Face Assignment
section.t: Face assignment uses a nearest-face-center lookup via dot product. The face whose center unit vector has the maximum dot product with the query point is the face containing the point. This is equivalent to finding the face whose center is closest in angular distance, and requires no table lookup or coordinate transformation beyond the initial Cartesian conversion.

section.name: Pentagon Sector Assignment
section.t: Each face is divided into 5 golden gnomon triangular sectors by connecting the face center to each of the 5 pentagon vertices. The pentagon vertices are the centroids of the 5 icosahedron triangles surrounding the face's corresponding icosahedron vertex. These vertices are precomputed as constants for each face.

For the reference implementation, the pentagon vertices are derived from the icosahedron face topology at compile time. The sector is found by testing the query point against each of the 5 spherical triangles (face_center, pv[i], pv[(i+1)%5]).

section.name: Recursive Subdivision
section.t: Given the face and sector, the query point is recursively assigned to child triangles. At each level the triangle is split into 4 children by connecting the midpoints of all three sides. The child containing the point is identified by the spherical containment test and its 2-bit index is recorded.

The tangent-frame projection used in the reference encoder (projecting onto the north/east tangent plane at the face center) is replaced here by exact spherical triangle subdivision. The spherical midpoint function is used to compute child vertices exactly on the sphere, eliminating distortion accumulation across subdivision levels.

section.name: Top-Level Encode Function
section.t: The encode function takes a WGS-84 coordinate and a desired length in bytes (1 to 8) and returns a populated RsdggsCell. The length parameter controls the resolution: 1 byte encodes face only; each additional byte adds 4 subdivision levels, or 2 bits per level with 4 levels per byte starting from byte 1 (accounting for the 3 bits of sector in byte 1).

section.name: Decode Function
section.t: The decode function extracts the face, sector, and subdivision level sequence from a populated RsdggsCell. It does not reconstruct the precise geographic coordinate — it returns the cell information sufficient for regulatory database lookup. Geographic coordinate recovery (computing the cell center) is a separate operation not required for regulatory compliance.

section.name: Boundary Proximity Helper
section.t: The boundary proximity function B(cell, band) from Section 9.3 is implemented as a database lookup returning the number of RSDGGS resolution steps to the nearest rule-set-changing boundary. The function signature is shown; the database backend is implementation-defined.
